0.title: The Magna Carta of Christian Liberty: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
0.overview:
Paul wrote to the Galatians in a state of controlled fury. He was angry not for himself but for them — and for the gospel. Every other letter he wrote to a church opens with thanksgiving or blessing to God; Galatians has neither. He moves immediately, in the very first verse, to defend his apostolic authority, and by verse 6 he is in open astonishment: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel.” The urgency that presses through every paragraph of this letter was born of Paul’s conviction that the gospel itself was at stake — not a peripheral issue but the very core of what he had preached and what they had received.

The crisis had been created by a group scholars call the Judaizers — Jewish Christians who insisted that faith in Christ was necessary but not sufficient. Gentile believers also needed to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic law in order to be fully accepted by God and fully included in God’s people. This seems, on the surface, like a minor addition: faith in Christ plus a few religious practices. But Paul saw it with total clarity for what it was: a fundamental contradiction of the gospel. If anything in addition to Christ is required for justification — even something God-given and ancient like circumcision — then Christ is no longer sufficient, grace is no longer free, and the cross is no longer enough. “If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21).

Where were these churches, and when did Paul write? Galatia was both an ethnic region in the north of Asia Minor, settled by Celtic tribes, and a Roman province that also took in the southern cities of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Some think Paul wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, whom he may have visited on his later journeys (Acts 16:6; 18:23), and date the letter in the mid-50s. The more likely reading is that he wrote to the southern churches he founded on his first journey (Acts 13–14): Paul normally used the Roman provincial names, and Acts tells us plainly about those churches and nothing about any in the north. On that reading the letter was written around AD 48, just before the Jerusalem Council, which would explain why Paul never mentions the Council’s decision (cf. 2:1). It may well be his earliest letter. Its message does not depend on the answer.

Galatians is structured in three movements. Chapters 1–2 are autobiographical: Paul defends the divine origin of his gospel (he received it not from men but from Jesus Christ directly) and recounts his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, where the gospel’s logic was at stake in a table-fellowship dispute. Chapters 3–4 are theological: Paul argues from Scripture (Abraham, the covenant, the law’s purpose, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah) that the gospel of grace by faith preceded the Mosaic law by 430 years and is not superseded by it. Chapters 5–6 are practical: the freedom of the gospel is not license for the flesh but the only true basis for life in the Spirit and love for the neighbor.

Martin Luther’s Commentary on Galatians (1535) is among the most celebrated commentaries in the history of the church. He called this letter his “Katie von Bora” — his beloved, the one he was married to. For Luther, Galatians was the text that articulated what the Reformation was about: the righteousness of God is not a demanding standard to be met but a free gift to be received. Justification is by faith alone, in Christ alone, by grace alone. Anything added to that formula is a subtraction from it.

Read Galatians as the most passionate defense of free grace in the entire canon. Every person who has ever felt that their standing before God depends on their performance needs to hear it. Every church that has drifted toward moralism — toward making the Christian life about spiritual self-improvement rather than trust in the finished work of Christ — needs to be dragged back to Galatians and made to sit with it until the gospel is clear again. Paul wrote it because the gospel is always under threat, and the threat almost always comes from the same direction: the desire to add something to Christ, to make grace a little less free, to make human effort a little more decisive. Galatians says: no. The cross is enough. Christ is enough. Grace is enough. “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

1.title: No Other Gospel: The Divine Origin of Paul’s Message
1.overview:
The letter begins with a defense of apostolic authority and immediately escalates to a declaration that would have shocked its first hearers: the gospel Paul preached is not of human origin, and anyone — even an angel from heaven — who preaches a different gospel is under divine curse. The word translated “accursed” is anathema — the strongest possible language of divine condemnation. Paul uses it twice in two verses (vv. 8–9), the repetition signaling that this is not rhetorical heat but deliberate, settled conviction.

The reason for the severity is simple: if the gospel can be modified by human authority — by apostles, by tradition, by ecclesiastical consensus — then it is not the gospel of God but the gospel of men. And the gospel of men, however sincerely presented, however religiously decorated, cannot save. Only the gospel that comes from God can bring a person into right standing with God. The divine origin of the gospel is therefore not an abstract theological claim; it is the practical ground of the gospel’s saving power.

Paul then makes his case autobiographically. He was not taught the gospel by the Jerusalem apostles; he received it directly from Jesus Christ, by revelation. The account of his conversion and his minimal contact with the Jerusalem church in the years that followed is not self-congratulation but an argument: his gospel is independently and divinely authenticated. It is the same gospel the Jerusalem apostles preach — but its authority does not rest on their endorsement. It rests on the revelation of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by stressing that his apostleship came not from any human source or appointment but directly from Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, the very point his opponents in Galatia disputed. Writing with the believers around him to the churches of Galatia, he wishes them grace and peace from God and from Christ, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, as the Father willed, and he gives glory to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as Eternal Initiative, Not Emergency Repair

The christological formula of vv. 3–5 is among the earliest in the New Testament, and it grounds the Reformed conviction that salvation originates wholly in God. The Son’s self-giving is voluntary; its object is our sins; its effect is rescue out of an age, not improvement within it; and its source is the Father’s own will. Two errors are shut out at once. The first makes the cross a late correction to a plan that went wrong — but Christ gave himself according to the will of our God and Father, and Peter preaches the same thing at Pentecost, that he was delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

The second sets a stern Father against a merciful Son, as though mercy had to be extracted from heaven by the death of Jesus. Verse 4 forbids it. The Father willed the giving; the Son gave himself; there is no division of sentiment in the Trinity toward sinners. Grace is not reactive. It is eternal initiative, and it terminates in glory to God (v. 5), which is where the letter will end up as well.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had received a complete gospel and were being told it was a foundation needing a second storey. Paul’s opening answers that before it is raised: the apostleship is unmediated (v. 1), the senders are a company and not a maverick (v. 2), and the gospel summarised in vv. 3–5 has no vacancy in it for a human contribution — Christ gave himself, and the Father willed it.

Now: The same instinct survives wherever the gospel is treated as the entry requirement and something else as the real content of the Christian life — a sacramental record, a moral achievement, an intensity of spiritual experience. The test is simple and can be run on a bad week: if approaching God after a week of failure feels materially different from approaching him after a good one, something has already been added, whatever is said out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead— and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul opens by insisting that he is an apostle sent directly by Jesus Christ and God the Father — not appointed by people or through any human go-between. Everything in this letter depends on that claim, because if his message came from Christ, nobody may amend it.

No warm-up. Paul normally names himself and his readers, then spends a warm paragraph thanking God for them. Not here. His credentials arrive in the first breath, wedged between dashes, and they are not modest.

An envoy. Apostolos means one who is sent, carrying the authority of the sender. A king’s messenger does not improve the message to suit the room; he delivers it and answers to the throne, not the audience.

Two doors closed. “Not from men” — no human being is the source of what he preaches. “Nor through man” — no human was even the delivery route. Someone in Galatia was evidently calling him a second-hand apostle: a man who got his gospel from Jerusalem and quietly dropped the awkward parts. Paul refuses the description in his first sentence.

“Who raised him from the dead.” This is load-bearing, not decoration. The Twelve were commissioned by a Jesus they had walked beside for three years. Paul was commissioned outside Damascus by a Jesus he had never met (Acts 9:3–6; 1 Corinthians 9:1) — and the only thing that makes that a commission rather than a hallucination is that the man is alive. Take out the resurrection and Paul is a zealot with a story.

Not alone, and not warm. “All the brothers who are with me” — this is not one man’s grievance dressed as doctrine. And “to the churches of Galatia” — his own congregations in the highlands of central Turkey, planted on his first journey through towns like Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, where he had been stoned and left for dead (Acts 13–14). He greets them with nothing: no “saints,” no “beloved.” Just the address, as on an envelope.

A test. Where does your confidence in the gospel actually rest? If on the preacher who first explained it, the church that raised you, or the tradition you have always trusted, then it can be revised by them — and sooner or later it will be, because all three are made of people. Paul insists his message has a different pedigree, and so a different durability. Make sure yours rests on Christ’s word, not on the people who passed it on.
verseByVerse.note: Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor. Many think the letter went to the churches Paul founded on his first journey — Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe; others think of ethnic Galatians farther north.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s greeting already preaches the gospel: grace and peace come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who freely gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age — as the Father willed. And Paul cannot finish the sentence without breaking into worship.

Grace, then peace. Greeks opened letters with chairein, “greetings”; Jews said shalom, “peace.” Paul bends the first into charis, grace — undeserved favour — and sets the Hebrew blessing beside it. Two worlds used these words daily and meant little by them, as we say “how are you?” without waiting. Paul fills them again. And the order never reverses in his letters: grace first, then peace. Peace is not the price of admission; it is what grace leaves behind.

“Who gave himself.” Not “was given” or “was taken.” In the garden twelve legions of angels were within reach, and a detachment fell backwards at his voice, and he handed himself over (Matthew 26:53; John 18:6). No one took his life; he laid it down (John 10:18). And “for our sins” — not for our disadvantages or unrealised potential, but for what is actually wrong. “For” carries the whole weight of the cross: in our place, the innocent where the guilty should stand.

Rescued from this age. “Deliver” means to snatch out — a rescue party pulling a man from a burning building, not a crew renovating it. Jewish teaching divided history into this present age and the age to come. Paul says the age to come has already broken in, and believers have been hauled out of the old one while still walking around inside it. Make that concrete: this is the age of bad scan results, of vows that end with lawyers, of trafficked children and old men dying alone — and of my own heart quietly preferring itself to God on a Tuesday morning. That is what Christ gave himself to pull people out of.

The Father’s will. The cross was not a late rescue plan, nor a reluctant Father talked round by a loving Son. The Son’s self-giving was “according to the will of our God and Father.” There is no reluctance anywhere in the Trinity toward sinners.

Worship before argument. “To whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.” Paul hasn’t begun his argument and already cannot get through his opening without stopping to adore. If your doctrine of grace doesn’t regularly stop you in mid-sentence to give thanks, read these three verses slowly today and let it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Instead of thanksgiving, Paul expresses astonishment that the Galatians are so quickly turning from the God who called them by grace to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all, only a distortion spread by people unsettling them. Anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one they received, even Paul himself or an angel, is under God’s curse; he says it twice. He is not trying to win human approval; if he were, he would not be Christ’s servant.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Stands Over the Church That Preaches It

The double anathema of vv. 8–9 establishes something the Reformers staked their lives on: the gospel is not the church’s property, to be developed by councils or refined by consensus. A message that human authority conferred can be amended by human authority, and would be. Paul therefore submits himself and heaven’s own courier to the same test he asks the Galatians to apply, which is not the prestige of the teacher but conformity to what was first delivered. Luther read these two verses and recognised the whole controversy of his century in them.

It should be added, because Paul’s own practice requires it, that the curse is not aimed at every disagreement among Christians: he allows real latitude on food and days and disputable matters (Rom. 14). What cannot be renegotiated is the ground of acceptance with God. And the reason nobody may edit this gospel is that it was bought, not drafted — there was an anathema in this story before Paul used the word, and it fell on the Son, becoming a curse for us (3:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were very probably sincere, and would have described themselves as the conservative party taking the Old Testament seriously. Circumcision was God’s own ordinance; the law was divinely given. They were not conscious apostates but well-meaning teachers who had inverted the relationship of law and grace — which is exactly why v. 10 matters, since sincerity was never the test.

Now: A different gospel rarely announces itself as one. It presents as the fuller, more serious, more culturally credible version. Two questions from this passage sort it out. Does this teaching change the ground on which a sinner is accepted by God, or only a secondary matter Christians have long disagreed about? And for a reader with a mother or a brother in such a church, the pastoral answer is in the grammar of vv. 8–9: the anathema falls on the one preaching, not on the sheep being misled.

verseByVerse.quote: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is astonished that the Galatians are so quickly deserting God, who called them by grace, for a “different gospel” — which is no gospel at all. Teachers have come who are distorting the good news, adding law-keeping to faith in Christ.

The missing thanksgiving. Every other letter Paul wrote to a church begins with thanks or blessing. Even the Corinthians — tolerating incest and drunkenness at the Lord’s Table — got a thanksgiving. The Galatians get this. It is the loudest silence in the New Testament letters, and the first readers heard it at once.

“I am astonished… so quickly.” The word can mean wonder or bewilderment; here it is bewilderment, and it was also a stock phrase of rebuke in ancient letters. Not years — Paul had preached, they had believed, the Spirit had come, and they were already most of the way to something else. A church can be evangelical on paper and lost in practice within a year.

Deserting a Person. “Deserting” is the word for changing sides — a soldier crossing to the enemy. Not a mistaken opinion but defection. And they are deserting not a doctrine but “him who called you in the grace of Christ.” You cannot leave the gospel of grace and keep the God of grace; he does not come apart from his message.

Can true believers desert Christ and be lost? Paul writes to the Galatians as to people he believes are Christ’s: “I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view” (5:10). Their danger was real, and the warning is the means God uses to bring them back; but those who are truly his do not finally fall away (cf. 5:4). The point of no return is the danger a church faces when it keeps the words and changes the gospel, not a sentence already passed on these believers.

Who were the troublers? They are usually called Judaizers. They were Jewish Christians who believed in Jesus, honoured the Scriptures, and taught that Gentile converts must also take on the marks of the law — circumcision above all, plus food laws and the sacred calendar — to be full members of God’s people (Acts 15:1, 5). Not Christ instead of Moses, but Christ plus Moses. They would have called themselves the conservatives, the ones taking the Old Testament seriously.

Not another gospel — an inverted one. “A different gospel — not that there is another one.” What they are turning to is not a second version of good news; it is not good news at all. “Distort” means to turn inside out. Adding law-keeping to grace does not top grace up; it reverses it. The moment my acceptance depends even one per cent on my performance, God is no longer the One who justifies the ungodly but the One who audits the diligent, and I am back keeping score.

A test. After a week of failure — short temper, prayerlessness, the same sin on Thursday — does approaching God feel different from after a good week? If so, something has already been added to the gospel, whatever you say aloud. That is how quietly this happens. Come to God tonight on exactly the same ground as after your best week: Christ alone.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers had come insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone — even Paul himself or an angel from heaven — preaches a gospel contrary to the one the Galatians received, let him be accursed. Paul says it twice. The gospel stands over every messenger; no one may change the ground on which sinners are accepted by God.

Anathema. “Accursed” is the Old Testament word for what was placed under the ban, devoted to God for destruction — Jericho, and Achan’s stolen silver (Leviticus 27:28–29; Joshua 7). It means handed over to God’s judgment. Paul uses this strongest word not about immorality in Corinth but here.

Impossible examples. “Even if we” — Paul puts himself first. If the man who planted these churches came back next spring with a revised message, they are to reject him. “Or an angel from heaven” — not a demon in disguise but heaven’s own courier. The gospel does not take its authority from its messenger.

Said twice, in cold blood. Verse 8 might be temper. So he repeats it: “As we have said before, so now I say again.” And the second time he drops “even if”: “if anyone is preaching.” Someone is.

Is every doctrinal disagreement damnable? No; Paul allowed real latitude on food and days (Romans 14). What he curses is a gospel contrary to the one received, and this letter shows which question he means: on what ground is a sinner accepted by God? Church government, details of the last days, the mode of baptism — Christians have argued these for centuries without either side being outside the faith. Change the ground of acceptance from Christ’s finished work to anything a person contributes, and the argument is no longer inside Christianity.

Does this include those who claim new revelation from an angel? Yes, and it is the plainest test the Bible gives. Joseph Smith said the angel Moroni led him to the Book of Mormon; Islam teaches that Gabriel gave the Qur’an to Muhammad. Paul anticipated exactly this: even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a different gospel, the messenger is cursed and the message rejected. No later revelation, however supernatural its claimed source, may contradict the gospel the apostles preached. Paul warns elsewhere that “even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor 11:14).

And what of churches like Rome? The test is the one Paul gives. The Council of Trent made faith, works and the sacraments together the ground on which a person is finally justified, and condemned those who teach justification by faith alone. That teaching falls on the wrong side of Paul’s line. Yet the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches also confess the Trinity, Christ’s deity, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, and many of their members trust Christ alone in spite of what their church teaches. The curse falls on the false gospel and those who preach it, not on everyone who sits under it, and our part is to make the true gospel plain to them.

“Is my mother accursed?” Someone has a mother in a church teaching something like this, or a brother who has gone somewhere that adds requirements to Christ. Look who is in the sentence: “let him be accursed” — the one preaching. The anathema falls on the teacher, not the troubled congregation. Paul calls the Galatians themselves “my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth” (4:19). A shepherd who shouts at a wolf is not shouting at the flock. Pray for your mother, and make the true gospel plain to her.

Why no one may edit it. There was already an anathema in this story, and it fell on the Son: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (3:13). He stood where the ban falls, to buy this gospel for sinners at the price of himself. It is not Paul’s to amend. It was paid for.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — handed over to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks whether he is trying to win people’s approval or God’s. If he were still trying to please people, he would not be Christ’s servant. A man owned by Christ cannot also be owned by other people’s opinions.

Answering a charge. His critics seem to have called him a crowd-pleaser — a travelling preacher who dropped circumcision because it was a hard sell to Gentiles, cutting the difficult bits to keep the numbers up. His answer is the passage they just read. A man trying to please people does not curse angels in paragraph three.

His scars are the argument. Later he settles it: “If I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” (5:11). Keeping circumcision was the obvious man-pleasing move. It would have pleased the synagogue, defused the opposition, and kept him out of prison. That was the option he refused.

One master. “I would not be a servant of Christ” — a doulos, slave, owned not employed. A slave has one master. To need the room’s approval is to take a second owner, and no one can be owned twice.

A test. Name the person whose disapproval would be hardest to bear — not hypothetically, the actual face: a father, a colleague, a grown child, certain people at church. Now ask what you have already softened, delayed or left unsaid to keep that face from changing. Everyone has such a face, and the troublers had found the Galatians’. A Gentile believer was told by impressive men from the mother church that he was a second-class Christian, with great relief on offer if he would submit. Bad theology usually travels on the back of a longing to be approved.

The comfort underneath. Paul’s freedom is not toughness of personality; it is the arithmetic of grace. A man whose acceptance is still being decided must manage everyone’s opinion, because any one of them might be the verdict. A man accepted in Christ has had the verdict given in advance, in his favour, at the cost of the cross — and every other opinion has been demoted to an opinion (1 Corinthians 4:3–4; Proverbs 29:25). The tyranny of what people think ends not when you win their approval but when their approval stops being the court. Say the thing you have been holding back, kindly, this week.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now argues from his own biography, and the argument is chronological. In vv. 11–12 he states the thesis: the gospel he preached is not man’s gospel; he did not receive it from any man, nor was he taught it. Those two verbs are the exact vocabulary of rabbinic transmission, the machinery that had made him a Pharisee, and he is saying it had nothing to do with this. (When he tells Corinth that he received and delivered the resurrection facts, there is no contradiction: the facts came from the church, the meaning and the commission came by revelation of Jesus Christ.)

Then the evidence. Verses 13–14 are his own record of shame produced as an exhibit: he persecuted the church beyond measure and tried to destroy it, the verb an army uses of a city it means to leave uninhabitable — and he was advancing beyond his peers, ahead of many of his own age, winning at the system he was in. Nobody defects from the top of a religion he is succeeding at into a message that gets him flogged. In vv. 15–16 the sentence turns and every verb becomes God’s: set me apart before I was born (before there was a person there to be good or bad), called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son — God’s delight, not his duty — and the commission to the Gentiles arrives in the same breath as the conversion.

The rest is a chronology of distance. Verse 17 has him going not to Jerusalem but to Arabia, the Nabatean kingdom, where he was evidently preaching hard enough to make an enemy of a king (2 Cor. 11:32–33). Verses 18–19 give the numbers that carry the argument: after three years, fifteen days, two men — and the verb translated visit means to get to know someone, not to be trained or certified by them.

Verse 20 breaks off into an oath, which tells us Paul was not merely disagreed with but called a liar. Verses 21–22 put him in Syria and Cilicia — home to Tarsus, and several years with nothing recorded — still unknown in person, literally unknown by face, to the very Judean churches he had once hunted. And vv. 23–24 close with the one sentence those churches kept repeating: he who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy. Their response was not to check his credentials. They glorified God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Effectual Calling, and Revelation: the Grammar of Grace

Verses 15–16 are among the most compact statements of sovereign grace in Paul. Three divine acts stand in order, and Paul initiates none of them: God set him apart before birth, called him by grace, and was pleased to reveal his Son in him. The setting apart echoes Jeremiah called before the womb and the Servant of Isaiah 49; there may also be a deliberate play on words, since aphorizō, to set apart, sounds against the name Pharisee, most likely from a root meaning the separated ones.

Paul had separated himself by rigorous effort and it made him dangerous; God had set him apart before he separated himself from anything, and set him apart for the Gentiles. The calling is effectual, not an invitation awaiting a reply — the last thing Saul intended on that road was conversion. And the revelation is in me, internal as well as external: he had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Grace that reaches a man riding in the opposite direction with warrants in his bag is not a reward for seeking. (cf. Rom. 8:29–30; Eph. 1:4–5)
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s critics could point to his absence from Jesus’ earthly ministry and his late arrival among the apostles. His reply is the chronology of vv. 17–22: he went to Arabia rather than Jerusalem, waited three years, stayed a fortnight, met two men, then vanished into Cilicia for years, and the Judean churches would not have recognised him in the street. If his gospel came from that world, its members would at least have known his face.

Now: A disqualifying history made into evidence (vv. 13–14), a calling that began before the one called was looking (v. 15), and hidden years that turn out to be part of the work (vv. 17, 21–22) — three things that reach an ordinary believer directly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wants the Galatians to know that his gospel is not a human message. He did not receive it from anyone or learn it from a teacher; it came to him by a revelation of Jesus Christ. A gospel from Christ cannot be amended by people.

“I would have you know, brothers.” A formula for what he most wants remembered — and a family word right after cursing angels. He is fighting for them, not with them.

Three closed doors. Not “man’s gospel” — not measured by a human standard or shaped to human taste. “I did not receive it from any man” — nobody handed it on. “Nor was I taught it” — he did not sit under anyone to learn it. “Received” and “taught” were exactly how a rabbi was made: tradition passed hand to hand, master to pupil — Gamaliel to Saul of Tarsus (Acts 22:3). Paul had that pedigree, and says the machinery that made him a Pharisee had nothing to do with this.

A fair problem. To Corinth Paul writes, “I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died… was buried… was raised” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Received from whom? From the church before him. Both are true. What he received from others were the facts — dates, burial, witnesses — things anyone in Jerusalem could tell him, and that he certainly heard from Peter. What no one gave him was their meaning and his commission. Before Damascus he knew Jesus had been crucified; he was persecuting people over it. What he could not be taught was that this crucified man is the Son of God, that his death ends the law as a way of acceptance, and that Paul must take this to the nations. That came by revelation.

“A revelation of Jesus Christ.” It can mean a revelation about Jesus or from him, and Paul probably means both, because on the Damascus road they were one event: the risen Christ pulled back the curtain, and behind it was himself.

Why it matters to you. A gospel from human consensus can be amended by human consensus; a committee that adopted it can update it next century. A gospel from Christ cannot be amended by anyone, because nobody in the discussion outranks him (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:20–21). That is the church’s security, and why a believer in first-century Galatia and you, on a Monday morning, stand on exactly the same ground. When someone offers you an updated gospel, ask who outranks Christ to make the change.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reminds the Galatians of his former life: he violently persecuted the church and tried to destroy it, and he was racing ahead in Judaism, fiercely zealous for his ancestors’ traditions. Nobody leaves the top of a system he is winning at for a message that gets him flogged — unless something has happened to him.

Three details, each worse. “I persecuted the church of God violently” — literally beyond measure, past where anyone was counting. “And tried to destroy it” — the word for what an army does to a city it means to leave uninhabitable. Luke supplies the pictures: Saul dragging off men and women to prison house by house (Acts 8:3); casting his vote for believers’ deaths; pursuing them to foreign cities “in raging fury against them” (Acts 26:10–11). There were families in Judea who still lived with it.

He was winning. “I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age” — the word means hacking a path forward, a pioneer’s word. He was not a failing religious man looking for something gentler; he was on the fast track. That is why he mentions it. The suggestion in Galatia was that Paul’s gospel was a softened Judaism, trimmed for people who couldn’t manage the whole thing. His answer: look at who I was. A man like that does not just change his mind. Something has to happen to him.

History made into evidence. Paul is not confessing here; he is citing. He puts the worst of his life on the table, calmly, in a letter to be read aloud in four towns. Some reader carries a history he has never said aloud — something done at twenty-two, something a family still lives with, something that surfaces at three in the morning arguing that whatever grace is for, it is not for that. Look at what has happened to Paul’s past. It has not been erased or explained away; he names it plainly. It has been made into evidence for the gospel. The worse the record, the better it proves that this message did not come from him.

The foremost. He said it later more simply: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him” (1 Timothy 1:15–16). The chief of sinners was kept alive on that road so that no one afterwards could say his own case was too far gone. If that is your fear, bring that history to Christ by name today.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then God — who had set Paul apart before he was born and called him by grace — was pleased to reveal his Son in him, so that he would preach Christ among the Gentiles. Every verb here is God’s. Paul did not seek God; God came for Paul.

Set apart before birth. Before the zeal, the persecution, the promising student — before there was a person to be good or bad. The language echoes the prophets: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5), and the Servant called “from the womb” (Isaiah 49:1). There may be a play on words: “set apart” may echo the root of the word Pharisee, “separated ones.” Paul had spent his life separating himself — from Gentiles, the unclean, the careless — and it made him the most dangerous man the church knew. God had set him apart before he separated himself from anything — and set apart, of all things, to go to the Gentiles.

“Called me by his grace.” Not because of his zeal or in spite of his record. The call had no cause outside God. And God’s call in Paul’s letters is not an invitation left awaiting a reply; it is the summons that raises the dead man it addresses. The last thing Saul intended, riding to Damascus with warrants, was to become a Christian.

“Was pleased.” It was God’s good pleasure, his delight — not a reluctant salvage. At the moment Acts describes Saul “still breathing threats and murder” (Acts 9:1), God is described as glad.

“In me.” Literally, “to reveal his Son in me.” Not only a bright light on a road, but something opened inside. He had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Now the Son himself was unveiled within him, and everything he knew rearranged itself around a living Person. And the commission came in the same breath: “in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles.” No probation period.

Is this about every believer, or only Paul? In the first place it is Paul’s own call to be an apostle, in words that echo Jeremiah, “before you were born I consecrated you” (Jer 1:5). But the same pattern holds for every believer: God chose his people “before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4) and calls them by grace (Rom 8:29–30). Some Christians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. Paul’s own case is the strongest answer: what God foresaw in Saul was a persecutor, and grace called him anyway.

A test. If you are troubled whether you chose God or he chose you, ask a simpler question: on the day it happened, was I looking for him? Paul was riding in the opposite direction with authority to arrest people who loved the name. If grace reached him there, grace is not a reward for seekers, and you need not audit the sincerity of your first steps to know whether you are safe (John 15:16). Heaven was not scandalised by Saul of Tarsus; it had made arrangements for him before his mother knew she was carrying him. Thank God today that he came for you.

parallels.desc: the LORD called me from the womb

verseByVerse.quote: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After his conversion Paul did not go to Jerusalem to the apostles before him; he went into Arabia and then returned to Damascus. His gospel was not learned at headquarters. And the hidden years that followed were part of God’s work, not a delay before it.

He went the other way. If his gospel had come from the Twelve, Jerusalem is where he would have gone at once — newly converted, untaught, with a lifetime of persecution to explain. He did not.

Arabia. Not an empty desert, whatever the paintings suggest, but the Nabatean kingdom south and east of Damascus — towns, trade routes, a capital at Petra, ruled by King Aretas. Paul lets slip what he did there: the governor under Aretas guarded Damascus to seize him, and he escaped over the wall in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Kings do not post guards for men quietly meditating. He had been preaching long enough to make an enemy of a monarch.

Three years off the map. The next verse says “after three years.” Three years between Damascus and his first conversation with Peter, with almost nothing recorded. Scripture does not say what happened, and it is better to admit that than to fill it in. What is certain is that the Paul who wrote Romans did not have Romans in his head on the Damascus road. Somewhere between the light and the letters, the Old Testament was rebuilt around Christ in that mind, and the only Teacher named is the Lord.

For the one in the waiting room. Some believers’ lives feel like a waiting room: gifts present and nothing asked; training done and the door never opened; illness taking the decade that was supposed to count. Someone at fifty cannot see what the twenty years since conversion were for, and suspects God has mislaid him. Scripture’s pattern runs the other way so consistently it is almost the rule. Moses had forty years in Midian minding sheep. David was anointed as a boy and then hunted through caves. Joseph went from dream to throne by way of a pit and a prison. The Son of God spent thirty years in a workshop and three in public. The hidden years are not the delay before the work; they are part of it, often the part that makes the rest possible. The apostle who wrote “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11) did not learn it by accident.

A test. Look at the stretch of your life that feels wasted. Ask not “why has nothing happened?” but “what has God been doing in me here that I could not have learned in public?” Then give him that year again, in prayer. God was no less involved in Paul’s silent years than in the light on the road; he simply wasn’t narrating them.
verseByVerse.note: Arabia here is the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three years later Paul went to Jerusalem to get to know Peter, stayed fifteen days, and saw no other apostle except James, the Lord’s brother. Every number makes his point: his gospel was not handed to him in Jerusalem.

To visit, not to be trained. “To visit” is a rare word Paul uses nowhere else: to go and get to know someone worth meeting. Not to be examined, trained, or commissioned. (Paul calls him Cephas, Peter’s name in Aramaic; both mean “rock,” the name Jesus gave him, John 1:42.)

Fifteen days. Long enough for two men to talk themselves hoarse; nothing like long enough to train an apostle, when everyone knew a rabbinic apprenticeship took years. One would like to have been in that house. Peter had denied the Lord by a charcoal fire and been restored by another (John 18:18; 21:9). Paul had hunted the people Peter pastored. Neither had a past to be proud of, and both had been handled by the same mercy. Those fifteen days surely included the eyewitness accounts — the boat, the courtyard, the shore — with a man who had seen none of it listening to every word.

James. Jesus’ brother, raised in the same house, who during the ministry did not believe (John 7:5). Then his brother was killed, and “he appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7). That meeting turned an unbelieving brother into the leader of the Jerusalem church, who calls him “the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1). It takes something considerable to make a man worship the boy he grew up beside.

Was James Jesus’ full brother? The plain reading is that he was a son of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brother. The early church developed other views, that he was Joseph’s son by an earlier marriage or a cousin, to protect the belief that Mary remained a virgin, but the New Testament never suggests either. And Paul’s “except James” shows that he counted James among the apostles in a wider sense; the risen Christ had appeared to him (1 Cor 15:7), and he became the leading elder at Jerusalem.

An honest difficulty. Luke says Barnabas brought Paul “to the apostles,” plural, and he went in and out among them (Acts 9:27–28). Paul says he saw none except James. Luke summarises in two verses and uses “the apostles” as a collective — Peter and James being the circle’s most prominent leaders — as someone who met the Prime Minister and the Chancellor might say he met the government. Paul, whose argument depends on the precise number, gives it. Both are true.

The point lands. If the Galatians want to believe Paul’s gospel was issued in Jerusalem, they must believe it was issued in a fortnight, three years too late, by two men who never claimed to have given it to him. And there is something here for you: Paul went to know Peter, not to be approved by him. Seek out older believers to learn from, but don’t make their approval the ground of your faith.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. James the Lord’s brother led the church in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul breaks off his account to swear before God that he is not lying. He is being called a liar about where his gospel came from, and the stakes are too high for a simple denial.

An oath in mid-story. Halfway through a plain account of dates, places and names, he calls God as witness. Nobody does that unless something is at stake. Paul was not merely debating people with different opinions. A rival account of his life was circulating in Galatia, detailed and plausible enough to stick: someone had told these churches a different story about where their founder got his message.

Didn’t Jesus forbid oaths? “Do not take an oath at all… Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:34–37; James 5:12). Look at what Jesus forbade. Oaths had become a sliding scale — swear by the temple and you may wriggle out; swear by the gold of the temple and you are bound (Matthew 23:16–22) — so that a man could signal how much of what he said he would stand behind, which made his ordinary word worthless. Christ abolishes the scale: a disciple’s plain yes carries the full weight of an oath. Paul is not grading his honesty. He is under formal accusation, testifying to a matter on which souls depend. Scripture is not embarrassed by that kind of solemn witness — Paul does it elsewhere (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23); God swore by himself to guarantee a promise (Hebrews 6:13–17); and Jesus answered under oath at his trial (Matthew 26:63–64).

He defends the gospel, not himself. Notice what Paul does not do. No wounded paragraph about his years of service, no list of what these churches owe him. He swears to one thing: the facts of where the gospel came from. A man defending his reputation protects his reputation. Paul lets his name take whatever damage it takes and puts the oath where the danger is. If the Galatians think Paul unimpressive, nobody is lost. If they think the gospel a human product, everything is.

A test. When you are criticised, what do you defend first — your reputation, or the truth? Next time, let your name take the knock and stand only where the gospel is at stake. And let your ordinary yes be as reliable as an oath, so that you seldom need one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul then went to Syria and Cilicia, and the churches of Judea did not even know him by sight. His gospel was not shaped by the Christian world closest to Jerusalem; they knew him only by report.

He went home. Cilicia is where Tarsus is. Luke explains why: Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem were trying to kill him, so the brothers sent him off to Tarsus (Acts 9:29–30). Then Acts carries on without him for years, until Barnabas goes to Tarsus to find him (Acts 11:25). Those years have no recorded sermon, named convert, letter or church — a striking silence about the man who wrote about a quarter of the New Testament.

Unknown by face. The Judean churches — the congregations he once hunted — wouldn’t have recognised him in the street. They were the churches closest to Jerusalem and most steeped in apostolic teaching. If Paul’s gospel had been absorbed from that world, they would at least have known what he looked like. They did not.

For the Christian with no audience. Most believers are unknown by face to almost everyone. The work is done in a house no one watches, in a job no one would write about, among two or three people who will never be famous either. The years in Cilicia produced no headline, and they produced the apostle to the Gentiles. Do today’s unseen work as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23).

Restoration at a distance. Paul is hidden from the very people he had wronged. He had helped put some of their members to death, and now they were praying for a man they would not have recognised. There is a kind of restoration God works at a distance, where the people harmed are not asked to manage the one who harmed them, and both are carried by the same grace without meeting.
verseByVerse.note: Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus.

verseByVerse.quote: They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Judean churches only kept hearing, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy” — and they glorified God because of him. The chapter ends not with Paul’s credentials but with worship of God.

The sentence they kept repeating. “They only were hearing it said” — continuous, the report going round the villages of Judea, told at every gathering the way a church tells the story it cannot get over. And “us”: it passed between the very people he hunted — families who had lost someone, congregations that had scattered. The man who set out to make sure this message didn’t survive was now carrying it across the empire.

The whole gospel in one line. A before and an after; a total change; a person who did not manage it himself; and evidence that is not what he says about himself but what he now does with his life.

“They glorified God because of me.” Literally, “in me.” Not “they were reassured about my credentials” or “they admired my transformation.” They looked at what had become of Saul and worshipped. He was evidence about God, and the evidence made them praise. Paul has spent twenty-four verses arguing that his gospel did not come from men. The Judean churches had settled it years earlier on one report — not by weighing credentials but by recognising an impossibility and knowing whose work it was.

A test. What would people who knew your “before” say about your “after”? Not your achievements, but what Christ has changed. If they would glorify God because of you, thank him. If not, ask him for a change that only he could produce — and let it be him they praise. The chapter that opened with a curse on angels closes with worship rising from villages that suffered at the hands of the man described, and its last word is glory — not Paul’s.
