2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the biographical argument’s climax and the letter’s theological turning point. Two episodes dominate: the Jerusalem conference (vv. 1–10), where the apostles affirmed Paul’s gospel of grace without requiring Gentile circumcision; and the Antioch confrontation (vv. 11–14), where Paul opposed Peter to his face because Peter’s behavior contradicted the gospel he believed. Both episodes illustrate the same point: the gospel of justification by faith alone is the non-negotiable centre of Christianity, and it must be defended even when the offender is the most respected leader in the church.

The chapter’s second half (vv. 15–21) is the theological centrepiece of the entire letter — the most concentrated statement of justification by faith in Paul’s letters apart from Romans 3. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” The verb “justified” (dikaioō) is a forensic term: to be declared righteous by the divine judge, to have one’s legal status before God established as “not guilty.” This declaration is made not on the basis of law-keeping (which can only expose and condemn sin) but on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ.

The chapter ends with the most luminous personal testimony in Paul’s letters: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” This is the gospel arriving at its destination: not merely a changed legal status but a transformed life — union with Christ, the old self crucified, the new life animated by faith in the one who loved and gave himself for me, personally, individually, sacrificially.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 opens with a number that is itself the argument: after fourteen years of preaching and planting without Jerusalem laying a hand on his message. He goes up with Barnabas, who had once vouched for him when the Jerusalem church would not go near him, and with Titus, an uncircumcised Greek — not a companion so much as an exhibit. In v. 2 he goes because of a revelation, not by summons, and meets the leaders privately rather than staging a public showdown he could have won.

His stated purpose, to make sure he was not “running in vain,” is easily misread as doubt about his gospel; chapter 1 forbids that. The danger he is guarding against is that the church might become two churches, a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms.

Verse 3 gives the verdict in one line: even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. With the test case standing in the room, Jerusalem did not require him to become a Jew. Verses 4–5 explain the pressure that made this a fight. The language is the language of espionage — false brothers secretly brought in, men who slipped in to spy out the freedom of the Gentile churches, whose stated object was slavery. Paul did not yield even for a moment, and gives a pastoral reason rather than a principled one: so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. Doctrinal firmness is a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free.

Verse 6 reports the outcome in a phrase — they added nothing to me — and grounds it in the fact that God shows no partiality, a principle Paul turns on the apostles themselves. Verses 7–8 set out the shape of the agreement: Paul entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised just as Peter to the circumcised, one gospel and two mission fields, with God himself named as the one who worked through both men. In v. 9 the order of the clauses carries the theology: the pillars first perceived the grace that was given and only then gave the right hand of fellowship — recognition of what God had done, not a handshake that conferred it. And v. 10 adds the single request Jerusalem made, that they remember the poor, which Paul was already eager to do.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Gospel, One People, One Way In

The Titus decision of v. 3 settles a question of the first order: justification is on identical terms for Jew and Gentile, and no covenant marker supplements faith at the point of acceptance with God. This is not a statement about cultural inclusion; it is a claim about the nature of justification itself, and the Reformed understanding of the covenant of grace — one covenant, one people, one Saviour, one way of entry — finds its clearest apostolic expression here.

Two further principles sit inside the passage. The word entrusted (v. 7) is a steward’s word, and it quietly disqualifies everyone in the dispute from editing the message: Paul may not adjust it to suit Gentiles and Jerusalem may not adjust it to suit Jews, for the same reason, which is that neither owns it. And the sequence of v. 9 — grace perceived, then fellowship extended — gives the church its permanent task in recognising anyone. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church perceives what God has given and says so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Galatia was being told that Gentile believers needed circumcision added to their faith. Paul’s answer is that he took this precise question to Jerusalem with an uncircumcised Greek at his side (vv. 1–3), and the men whose authority the Judaizers were invoking added nothing (v. 6) and shook his hand (v. 9). The Judaizers are not following the Jerusalem apostles; they are contradicting them.

Now: Anything may be done for the gospel; nothing may be added to it — which is why Paul could later circumcise Timothy (Acts 16:3) and would not let anyone touch Titus. The same test still sorts real questions from false ones. Where a practice is offered as helpful, Christians may differ; where it is required for full acceptance, the gospel is at stake. And v. 10 guards the other flank: having refused to add one item to the gospel, Paul accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because that is not an addition but what grace does once it has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fourteen years later Paul went up to Jerusalem by revelation, with Barnabas and Titus, and privately laid out his gospel before the church’s leaders — not because he doubted it, but so that his work among the Gentiles would not be undone by a split church.

Fourteen years. The number is the argument: fourteen years of preaching and planting churches without the Jerusalem apostles laying a hand on his message. If his gospel needed their sign-off, it had worked without it for over a decade.

Three details. Barnabas is the man who vouched for Paul when Jerusalem wouldn’t go near him (Acts 9:27). Titus is a Greek, uncircumcised, walked into a meeting about whether Greeks must be circumcised — not a companion but an exhibit. And “because of a revelation” — he was sent, not summoned, and his nerve had not failed.

Privately. He went to the leaders first, in a closed room, rather than staging a public showdown he could have won. That is what a man who is right does with his rightness: he chooses the room where a thing can be settled over the platform where it gets performed. Take a disagreement to the person privately before you take it anywhere else (Matthew 18:15).

“Those who seemed influential.” It sounds like a sneer, and Paul is not overawed. But he isn’t attacking Peter and James; he will call them pillars and shake their hands. He refuses one thing: that reputation is what makes a gospel true. The troublers traded on Jerusalem’s prestige. Paul grants Jerusalem everything except the right to be the reason.

“Not… in vain.” This doesn’t mean Paul doubted his message; chapter 1 forbids that. The danger was that the church would become two churches — circumcised and uncircumcised, each with its own apostle and terms — and everything he had built would come apart in a generation. He was protecting the unity his doctrine requires.

Which visit? Acts records several. Many take this to be the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15. Others take it as the earlier famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30, which would mean Galatians was written before the Council. The second view has a strong argument: Paul describes a private meeting, not a public assembly, and if a formal apostolic ruling on circumcision already existed, it is hard to see why Paul, fighting on exactly that issue, never quotes it. The second view is more likely, fitting the southern Galatian churches of Acts 13–14 and a date around AD 48. But nothing in the argument depends on it. What matters is what happened in that room.
verseByVerse.note: It is debated whether this visit is the famine visit of Acts 11 or the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery— to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised. False brothers had slipped in to spy on the believers’ freedom in Christ and bring them into slavery, but Paul did not yield to them for a moment — so that the truth of the gospel would be kept for the Galatians.

The verdict in one line. The apostles looked at an uncircumcised Gentile believer and did not require him to become a Jew. If the troublers were right, Jerusalem had a duty to say so with Titus standing there. It said nothing of the kind.

But Timothy? Paul later circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3). The difference is everything. Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer (16:1), so he was already reckoned a Jew by birth, and nobody was demanding circumcision as a condition of salvation; Paul did it so Timothy could get into synagogues to preach. Titus was a Gentile, and it was being demanded as a requirement for acceptance with God. Paul’s rule: anything may be done for the sake of the gospel; nothing may be added to it. The moment a thing stops being free and starts being necessary, he will die on that hill.

Espionage. The words are spies’ words: “secretly brought in,” “slipped in,” “spy out.” Not honest men with a different opinion who lost an argument, but men gathering intelligence on how free the Gentile churches were.

“To bring us into slavery.” The whole letter in a phrase. What was offered looked like promotion — full membership, proper standing. It was chains. Anything that makes acceptance with God depend on performance puts a person on a treadmill, because the performance is never finished and the verdict never in.

Not for a moment. No diplomatic hour, no temporary allowance. Compromise never presents itself as surrender, only as a small, reasonable, temporary allowance for peace. Paul knew what the first inch was worth.

“For you.” “So that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you” — not so Paul might win, but for Gentile converts hundreds of miles away who would never know the meeting happened. That is what doctrinal firmness is for. Paul is not a man who enjoys a fight but a man standing in a doorway so that those behind him can stay free, and the freedom of every Gentile believer since came down that corridor (5:1).

A test. Where are you being asked to add something to Christ as a condition of belonging — a practice, a badge, a tradition? Enjoy it freely if it is good, but refuse it the moment it is made necessary for acceptance with God.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised — a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jerusalem leaders added nothing to Paul’s gospel. They saw that God had entrusted him with the gospel to the Gentiles just as he had entrusted Peter with it to the Jews — and that the same God was at work in both. One gospel, two mission fields.

“Added nothing.” Two words in Greek, and they end the argument. The troublers said Paul’s gospel was incomplete. The pillars heard it in full and had no correction, supplement or condition. Whatever the Galatians were told was missing, the men supposedly holding it did not think so.

God shows no partiality. The Old Testament says God does not lift up faces or side with the important man because he is important (Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7). Paul turns it on the apostles themselves. Peter had walked with Jesus and Paul had not, and it makes no difference to the question, because God is not impressed by credentials. That frees everyone: nobody in the room outranks the truth.

They saw. They did not add because they looked at the evidence. Something had plainly been happening in the Gentile world, and it was not Paul’s doing.

Entrusted. The word of a steward handed what belongs to someone else. It settles the dispute: someone entrusted with a message has no authority to revise it. Paul can’t edit this gospel to please Gentiles, and Jerusalem can’t edit it to please Jews, for exactly the same reason. Neither owns it. One gospel, two fields — not two gospels, and not a senior apostle with a junior assistant.

The third party. “He who worked through Peter… worked also through me.” Not Peter worked, or Paul, but God, the only one doing anything. That is why the comparison never becomes competition: two men used, one God working, and results in Jerusalem and Galatia with exactly the same Author.

For the discouraged servant. If you have measured your ministry against someone else’s and come away discouraged — the teacher with a small class beside the full hall, the parent whose children came slowly to faith beside the family where it seemed easy — the verse does not say the two men were equally gifted. It says one God worked in both. He is not divided among his servants, spending himself heavily on the impressive and thinly on the rest. Do your work this week as his, and leave the comparing to him.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When James, Peter and John — the church’s “pillars” — recognised the grace God had given Paul, they gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship: Paul to the Gentiles, they to the Jews. Their only request was that they remember the poor, which Paul was eager to do.

Recognition, then fellowship. They saw the grace first; then gave the hand. Reverse the clauses and the theology changes, as if the handshake conferred something. It acknowledged what God had already done. That is how the church recognises anything: ordination does not manufacture a minister, nor a handshake a brother. The church perceives what God has given and says so publicly. Where grace is evidently at work, acknowledge it; where it is not, no ceremony will supply it.

Pillars. The men on whom the weight rests. This James is the Lord’s brother (the apostle James, John’s brother, had been executed by Herod, Acts 12:2).

The right hand of fellowship. An open right hand holds no weapon; it says, between us this is finished. “Fellowship” is koinōnia, partnership — a joint stake in one enterprise, not merely a truce. Consider the room: the apostle who had hunted Christians and the apostle who had denied Christ in a courtyard put their hands together over a gospel neither had earned. The church is a company of forgiven enemies who have stopped competing for a standing never theirs to win. Nobody in that handshake had a record worth defending, which is what made it possible.

A division of labour, not of message. “We should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised” — never watertight, since Peter opened the Gentile door (Acts 10) and Paul went to the synagogue in every town.

Remember the poor. After a meeting about circumcision, law and salvation, the one request is that the poor not be forgotten, and Paul was already eager. He meant it: years of his life went into the collection for famine-struck Judean believers (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Paul refused to add one item to the gospel and accepted this obligation without a murmur, because it is not an addition. Nothing has been placed between a sinner and God. It is what grace does once it arrives. A church that understands justification by faith alone and has no interest in the hungry has not understood it (James 2:15–17; 1 John 3:17). Who among the poor will you remember this month — by name, with money or time?
verseByVerse.note: Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church. The poor were the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recounts how he confronted Peter at Antioch. Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he drew back and separated himself, afraid of the circumcision party, and other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed his lead in this pretence. Paul saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, so he challenged Peter publicly: if you, a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you force Gentiles to live like Jews?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Governs the Feet, Not Only the Confession

Peter’s failure was not doctrinal. He had proclaimed the equality of Jew and Gentile before God and won the argument for it. What v. 14 exposes is a gap between a confession genuinely held and a life not walking in line with it — which is what hypocrisy means in Paul’s usage, not the cynical pretence of faith one does not have. The Reformers’ principle that the church is always to be reformed by the gospel bites here: the gospel must govern table habits, social pressure and power dynamics, not merely statements of faith.

There is a further point of some weight. Peter is treated in this passage as a fallible man who can be publicly withstood and corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel — and Scripture records it without embarrassment. Whatever authority the Jerusalem leadership had, it was never authority over the message, which is precisely the argument of vv. 6–9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch was socially motivated, not theologically: v. 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the same snare Paul named at 1:10 — am I trying to please man? — and it swept up the whole Jewish contingent and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now:Two things in this section reach a reader directly: the room in which he is a slightly different Christian, and the question of when a leader should be confronted in public. Paul’s case meets every condition at once — public conduct, the gospel itself at stake, others being carried away, and the rebuke spoken to Peter’s face rather than about him — and the friendship survived it (2 Pet. 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Antioch Paul opposed Peter to his face, because he was clearly in the wrong. Peter had been eating with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he withdrew and ate separately, afraid of the circumcision party. He did not change his belief — only his seat, because of who was watching.

To his face. Not a letter or a word afterwards, but face to face, in front of everyone. “He stood condemned” is a courtroom phrase: not that Paul condemned him, but that he already stood condemned by the contradiction between his belief and his behaviour. Paul only read out the sentence.

The table. Eating together was not casual. A shared table meant shared life and acceptance. For a Jew to sit at a Gentile meal declared that the wall had come down, and Peter had been doing it meal after meal before the whole church.

Gradual. “He drew back and separated himself” — two gradual verbs, like a soldier giving ground. No announced policy. He just began sitting elsewhere, and everyone knew what it meant. “Fearing the circumcision party.” Not conviction; he had not changed his mind about anything.

How was this possible? This is the man who heard on the rooftop, “What God has made clean, do not call common,” who watched the Spirit fall on Gentiles in Cornelius’s house, and who defended it before Jerusalem and won (Acts 10–11). He was the leading expert on exactly this point. So knowing a truth and having settled it publicly does not immunise anyone against abandoning it when the wrong people walk in. It is the same Peter who knew who Jesus was and denied him to a servant girl by a fire. The mechanism hadn’t changed in twenty years: not doubt or argument, but the weight of a watching face. Fear of man is not a beginner’s sin that maturity leaves behind.

Peter’s authority. If Peter could be wrong on a matter of the gospel and publicly rebuked by another apostle, then no office of Peter’s is above correction by the gospel. Roman Catholic teaching limits papal infallibility to formal definitions, not conduct; but the point here is wider. The gospel judges Peter, not Peter the gospel, and that is true of every church leader since.

“From James.” This has been used to blame James, probably unfairly. Jerusalem later wrote to Antioch about men who had gone out and unsettled them “although we gave them no instructions” (Acts 15:24). Men who claim a great name aren’t always carrying it.

A test. Everyone has a room where he is a slightly different Christian — the workplace where faith goes quiet, the family table where a conviction isn’t mentioned, the old friends where the language changes. Peter didn’t deny the gospel at Antioch. He moved to a different table when certain people were watching, and Paul calls that standing condemned. Name your room, and decide now how you will sit there next time.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church. Eating together was the test: strict Jews would not share a table with Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The other Jewish believers joined Peter’s hypocrisy, and even Barnabas was carried away. Because their conduct was out of line with the truth of the gospel, Paul confronted Peter in front of them all: you live like a Gentile yourself — how can you force Gentiles to live like Jews?

Acting a part. “Hypocrisy” comes from the theatre: playing a role. Paul isn’t accusing them of secret unbelief, but of behaving in a way their convictions didn’t support because the audience had changed.

Even Barnabas. The “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36), who stood up for Paul when Jerusalem thought him a plant, fetched him from Tarsus, and travelled the first journey at his side. That detail is not to shame Barnabas but to show how strong the current was. No argument is recorded. It took a few significant people sitting at a different table, and the whole church moved.

Their feet were wrong. “Not in step with the truth of the gospel” — not walking straight. Their doctrine was fine; every man at those tables would have signed the same confession. The gospel is not only to be believed accurately but walked in, and it can be denied by a seating plan as effectively as by a sermon.

A trap with no exit. Peter had been living freely, so he plainly didn’t believe the food laws still bound him. Yet by withdrawing he told Gentile believers that to have his company they must take on rules he himself had stopped keeping. Nobody said it aloud. That is the force of “force”: pressure needn’t be spoken to be applied.

Should a Christian confront leaders publicly? Usually not. Jesus’ instruction is to go privately first and widen the circle only if there is no repentance (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul tells Timothy not to admit a charge against an elder except on two or three witnesses, and adds: “As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all” (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Here four things lined up, which rarely happens: the conduct was public, so a private word couldn’t undo it; the matter was the gospel itself, not a preference; others were already being swept away; and Paul said it to Peter’s face, at cost to himself — not about him, afterwards, to someone else. That last is the test most often failed. Much that calls itself courage in the church is a message to a third party or a post about a man who will never be in the room. Paul’s way is harder and kinder: say it where the person can answer.

The friendship survived. Years later Peter wrote of “our beloved brother Paul… according to the wisdom given him,” admitting that his letters contain “some things… that are hard to understand” (2 Peter 3:15–16). No bitterness. Two forgiven men could survive being told the truth. If you need to correct someone, do it to their face, about what matters, and keep loving them afterwards.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul spells out the principle. Even Jewish believers know that no one is justified by doing what the law requires but only through faith in Jesus Christ, so they too have trusted Christ in order to be justified by faith. If seeking justification in Christ shows that we are still sinners, that does not make Christ a servant of sin; rebuilding the law as a way of standing with God is what makes a person a transgressor. Through the law Paul died to the law so that he might live for God. He has been crucified with Christ; his life now is Christ living in him, and he lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him. He will not set aside God’s grace, for if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith: The Article by Which the Church Stands or Falls

Protestant theology came to call justification by faith articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae, the article by which the church stands or falls — a summary of Luther’s own conviction — and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is forensic — a declaration of status, not an infusion of goodness, though transformation certainly follows. It is by faith alone, its object is Christ alone, and it is by grace alone; and the Reformed tradition has always insisted the three stand or fall together. If faith is not the exclusive instrument, it is not by grace; if Christ is not the exclusive object of faith, it is not grace either.

One point of translation deserves noting since a reader may meet it. The phrase rendered faith in Jesus Christ in v. 16 can also be read as “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ” — his own obedience to the cross as the ground of acceptance. The majority Reformed rendering takes it as faith directed toward him; either way, faith is not a work that earns the verdict but the empty hand that takes it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). The argument from the insider to the outsider is conclusive: if the law cannot justify those to whom it was given, it will not justify anyone else. And v. 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into a wall that had been pulled down.

Now:The person who comes to faith from a life of moral respectability and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on identical ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability is as irrelevant to the verdict as the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Jews by birth know that no one is justified — declared right with God — by works of the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ. So they too believed in Christ, to be justified by faith and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.

The centre of the letter. The sentence the Reformation was built on, said three times in one verse because everything else stands on it.

“Justified” is a courtroom word. To justify is not to make someone good but to declare him in the right. A judge who justifies a defendant does not improve or educate him; he pronounces a verdict, and the man walks out with a status he did not have. We instinctively think of salvation medically — God as physician gradually curing us, with heaven at the end if the treatment works. Justification is not the doctor’s slow progress but the judge’s verdict, given whole, at the beginning. God also heals those he acquits, for a lifetime; but he does not acquit them because the healing is going well.

Works of the law. First, the deeds Moses’ law required, especially the markers that separated Jew from Gentile — circumcision, food laws, holy days, the very issues at Antioch. But Paul’s conclusion is wider: “by works of the law no one will be justified” (v. 16; cf. Psalm 143:2). Not the Gentile without the law, nor the Pharisee who kept it better than his peers. The law is holy, but it is a mirror, and a mirror has never washed a face.

The insiders came the same way. “We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners” is reasoning, not boasting. The most advantaged religious people on earth — covenant, Scriptures, temple, a lifetime of training — had to come the same way as outsiders. If the law could justify anyone, it would have justified them; instead they abandoned the attempt and trusted a crucified man.

What of the New Perspective on Paul? Scholars such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright argue that “works of the law” means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart, circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath, and that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people. They are right about the occasion: at Antioch the issue was table fellowship and identity markers. But Paul’s conclusion is wider than the occasion: “by works of the law no one will be justified.” Justification is a courtroom verdict on a guilty sinner, and the law condemns all who rely on it (3:10). Belonging to God’s people follows from that verdict; it is not what the verdict means.

Paul and James. But James says “a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (Jas 2:24). Do the apostles contradict each other? No. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is declared righteous before God, and answers: by faith, apart from works. James asks how a claim to faith is shown to be real, and answers that “faith apart from works is dead” (Jas 2:26). Paul opposes works as the ground of acceptance; James opposes a faith that is only words. Paul agrees that true faith works, “faith working through love” (5:6). We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

Faith in Christ, or Christ’s faithfulness? The phrase can also be read “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ,” meaning his perfect obedience justifies. There is truth in that: his faithfulness is the ground. But the majority Reformed reading takes it as our faith in him, and the next clause supports it: “so we also have believed in Christ Jesus.” Either way: the doing is his; the receiving is ours, and the receiving is not a contribution. Faith is the empty hand that takes the verdict.

A test. Ask what would have to be true for God to be pleased with you by Friday. If the honest answer involves a better performance than this week’s, you are trusting something other than Christ. The verdict was never waiting on Friday. It was given at the cross, received by faith, and it does not move (Romans 3:20–24; Philippians 3:8–9).

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul answers an objection: if seeking to be justified in Christ means we Jews are found to be “sinners” — having stopped living by the law — does Christ then promote sin? “Certainly not!” Whatever is wrong when a believer sins, Christ did not put him up to it.

The objection. If a man is accepted by faith rather than obedience, obedience doesn’t finally matter. And look what happened: Jewish believers stopped keeping food laws and started eating with Gentiles; by the law’s reckoning they became sinners. So Christ has turned observant men into law-breakers. Is he a servant of sin — running its errands?

“Certainly not!” Paul’s strongest negative, for suggestions to be thrown out rather than weighed. But notice what he doesn’t say. He doesn’t say grace makes sin unimportant, or that a justified person is no longer a sinner. He says the fault cannot lie where the objection puts it.

An insult to a Person. To call Christ a servant of sin slanders the One who died to destroy it — who took its whole weight into his own body and went into the dark under it. Paul reacts as anyone reacts when an absent friend is slandered.

A strange compliment. This objection has followed free grace ever since. Paul met it in Rome too: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” (Romans 6:1). If a preacher has never been accused of making grace too free, it is worth asking whether he has preached it. Paul, preaching it exactly right, was accused constantly.

The real answer. Not a retreat into rule-keeping but a question about what happened to the person. Grace doesn’t leave a sinner where it found him with changed paperwork. It puts him to death and raises him, and a man who has died to something doesn’t go back to it as though nothing happened. That is where vv. 18–20 go — to a cross, not a code of conduct. If you are using grace as permission, look at the cross until you can’t.

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Paul rebuilt the system of law-keeping he had torn down, he would prove himself a transgressor. Through the law he died to the law, so that he might live to God. The law did its job: it showed him he could not live by it, and handed him over to Christ.

Rebuilding the demolished. Picture a man who spent years building, judged the building unsound, and pulled it down. Now he goes back and puts every stone up again. He hasn’t merely wasted time; he has declared the demolition a crime. What Paul tore down was acceptance by performance — advancing beyond his peers, building his own righteousness. The transgression would not be leaving the law behind but going back to it as the way of acceptance. And he aims it at Antioch: Peter had been living in the gospel’s freedom and had begun laying stones back, one meal at a time.

“Through the law I died to the law.” The law itself was the instrument. It came to a man doing rather well and kept raising the standard until it had him: not just murder but anger; not just adultery but the look; not just the deed but the desire (Matthew 5:21–28). It kept speaking until the promising Pharisee understood he wasn’t ahead of anyone, that the machine he trusted was designed to convict him, and that on those terms he was a dead man. The law did what God gave it to do. It killed him — so he could stop trying to live by it (Romans 7:4).

The ache is the law at work. Nobody comes to Christ while his own account still looks solvent. The ache under religious striving — never enough, the standard always moving, a good week only a reprieve — is not a malfunction. It is the law doing its work, and its work is not cruelty. It is the last kindness of a guardian who intends to hand the pupil over to Someone else (3:24).

“So that I might live to God.” That is what the demolition was for: not to leave a man in the rubble but to get him out from under a life spent proving himself, into a life lived toward God. A test: is there a stone you have quietly put back — a rule, a record, a performance you are relying on to feel accepted? Take it down again today, and live toward God as someone already accepted.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.” Paul’s old self — living for its own record — died with Christ. Now he lives his ordinary life by trusting “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.”

A completed death. The tense is a past act whose results stand. Not “I am dying daily” or “I try to crucify myself.” It happened. When Christ died, Paul died, because Christ died as a representative, as Adam acted for a race, so that what happened to him happened to all joined to him (Romans 6:6). And Paul says “crucified,” not merely “died” — a criminal’s public death with no standing left. The impressive old self, with its record and rising reputation, did not retire honourably. It was executed.

Not erased. “It is no longer I who live” can sound as though Paul has been emptied out and replaced. Two things forbid that. The next clause: “the life I now live” — there is still an “I.” And the letter itself: the most personality-drenched document in the New Testament, its author angry, tender, sarcastic and affectionate by turns. Grace did not flatten Saul into a generic believer. It killed what he was living for and left him more himself than before. What died was the self that had to be somebody. What lives is a man indwelt (Colossians 3:3–4).

Monday. “The life I now live in the flesh” — in the body, with a stomach, a temper and a tentmaking business. Not an elevated spiritual condition.

By faith, not feeling. People who love this verse sometimes expect it to feel like something and are troubled when it doesn’t. Paul doesn’t say he lives by a sense of Christ’s presence or by spiritual experiences. He lives “by faith” — trusting a Person he cannot see, on days when nothing is felt. The indwelling is a fact about where Christ is, not a report on how you are doing.

“Who loved me.” The grammar turns singular. After a chapter of councils, delegations and mission fields, it ends with one man saying “me” twice — the same Paul who dragged women to prison (Acts 8:3). The cross is wide enough for the world and narrow enough to have a single name on it. Christ loved not humanity in the abstract but this man, with this record, while it was still being written. And he did not send help; he gave himself — the gift that costs the giver everything (Ephesians 5:2; 1 John 3:16).

A test. Say the last clause aloud with your own name in it: “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” Then live today’s ordinary tasks by trusting him — not by checking how you feel — as a man already dead to his old record and alive with Christ in him.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul does not set aside God’s grace. “For if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.” Adding anything human to Christ’s work implies the cross was unnecessary.

Who is annulling what. “Nullify” means to set aside, to treat a legal instrument as void. Paul was being accused of treating God’s law as nothing; he answers that the other side are annulling something, and it is not the law. It is grace.

The argument. Suppose there is any route to being right with God that runs through human obedience — even a small one, even as a supplement to grace. Then God had a way to save people without his Son’s death. And then Calvary was not a rescue but the most appalling waste in history: a Father watching his Son die in the dark for something that could have been managed another way.

Why Paul’s temper isn’t disproportionate. The troublers thought they were adding rigour to a message gone soft. Paul shows what their addition implies about the cross. You cannot say “Christ plus my performance” without saying underneath that his performance was insufficient, and the cross does not survive being called a supplement. “For no purpose” means gratuitously, for nothing — what every religion of human achievement ends up saying about the crucifixion, whether it means to or not (Hebrews 10:11–14).

There was no other way. If there had been, he would have taken it. He asked in the garden, three times, whether there was (Matthew 26:39–44). There was not. He went to the cross because nothing less would do, knowing the cost, and he did not die for nothing. He died for sinners, and it worked, and it is finished.

A test. What are you tempted to add to Christ to feel secure — your record, your religious habits, your church, your moral progress? Each of those, made a condition, says the cross was not enough. Thank God today that it was, and rest your whole weight on it.

Certainly not!<sup>18</sup>For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor.<sup>19</sup>For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.<sup>20</sup>I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.<sup>21</sup>I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological heart of Galatians: a sustained argument from Scripture that the gospel of grace by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the foundation on which all of God’s dealings with Abraham and his descendants have always rested. The law came 430 years after the Abrahamic covenant. It cannot therefore revoke the promise made to Abraham; it operates within a different register, serving a different purpose, pointing toward its own fulfillment and supersession in Christ.

Paul opens with an emotional appeal: the Galatians had experienced the Spirit. They knew it. Signs and wonders had accompanied their conversion. Did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The answer is obvious — and the answer settles the question about the ground of their acceptance with God. The same Spirit-receiving faith that initiated their Christian life is also the ongoing basis of their standing. Maturity in Christ is not a movement from faith toward law; it is a deepening of faith in the one in whom all the law finds its fulfillment.

The chapter’s christological climax is the most audacious claim in the letter: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (v. 13). The cross was not merely a sacrifice; it was a specific legal exchange. Christ took the law’s curse — the curse pronounced on all who fail to keep it perfectly — onto himself, becoming the accused on behalf of the accused, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has finished defending his apostleship and turns on the Galatians themselves, and the first line has no courtesy in it. In v. 1 he calls them un-minded and asks who has bewitched them, when what had been placarded before their eyes was Jesus Christ crucified. Then, instead of an argument, he asks about their own biography. Verse 2 puts the one question he says is sufficient: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? They knew the answer. They were, for the most part, uncircumcised pagans who heard and believed, and God moved in.

Verse 3 exposes the folly precisely: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Not sin — religion; the whole realm of what a man can do, mark and show. Verse 4 asks whether their suffering was wasted, and then Paul cannot finish the sentence. Verse 5 makes the question present tense: God is still supplying the Spirit and working miracles among them, and the evidence stands in the room while the argument goes on.

The sentence of v. 5 runs on a dash straight into v. 6, so Abraham is not a new topic but the last clause of the question. Genesis 15:6 is quoted: Abraham believed God and it was posted to his account as righteousness. Verse 7 draws the conclusion that overturns the whole Judaizing offer — it is those of faith who are Abraham’s sons. Verse 8 goes further: Scripture pre-gospelled Abraham, so the Gentiles were in view in God’s first sentence to him. And v. 9 sets every believer alongside the patriarch himself: blessed along with Abraham, on the same footing, in one queue.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Is Received by Faith, and the Reception Settles Everything

The appeal of vv. 2 and 5 is not to religious feeling but to a fact of record: the mechanism by which God gives his Spirit. Reformed theology has always held that the Spirit is the agent of union with Christ and that union with Christ is received by faith alone; here Paul argues it backwards from experience. If the Spirit came through the hearing of the gospel and not through law-works, then the law-works were never the channel, and no later addition can make them one.

The force of v. 3 is that the Christian life is not two-stage. There is no beginning by grace followed by an advance by performance. What justifies also sanctifies, and it is the same Spirit received in the same way from first to last. And vv. 6–9 place this outside the new covenant altogether: Abraham was justified by faith in Genesis 15, two chapters and many years before the sign of circumcision was given in Genesis 17. Justification by faith is not a Christian innovation. It is how God has always dealt with sinners.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were not asking the Galatians to abandon Christ. They were offering completion — take the mark, keep the calendar, and become full sons of Abraham like us. From inside, it looked generous and it looked mature. Paul’s answer in vv. 1–5 is to make them look at their own conversion: nothing in their hands, no circumcision, no Sabbath kept, and God gave them his Spirit. Then vv. 6–9 take Abraham, the Judaizers’ own trump card, and turn it over.

Now: Almost no believer decides to be justified by works; the drift of v. 3 is quieter than that. Over a few years the empty hands fill with real and often good things — a devotional habit, a serving rota, a reputation — and the ground of confidence migrates without anyone noticing the day it moved. The test is the one v. 2 implies. Think of your worst week, and ask whether God was as pleased with you that Sunday as on your best. If something flinches, the flinch is the answer, and vv. 6–9 are the cure: one queue, one way in, and Abraham himself is standing in it.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?” Jesus Christ crucified had been set before their eyes as plainly as a public notice. Now something has drawn their gaze away from the cross, and they have not noticed it moving.

“Foolish.” Not stupid but “un-minded” — people with good brains who have stopped using them on the one subject where everything is at stake. A man can hold a degree and read the markets correctly every morning and still be foolish about the gospel.

“Bewitched.” The word comes from the evil eye — the malign look thought to wither a crop or sicken a child. Paul doesn’t believe in spells. He reaches for the only category that fits: something has come over them that ordinary argument doesn’t explain. They have not been out-reasoned; they have been charmed. Two sights compete for one congregation — the bewitching look and Christ crucified. Whichever you keep looking at will shape you.

A public notice. “Publicly portrayed” means placarded, posted in a public place. In a Galatian town a governor’s ruling or a notice about a runaway slave went up in the marketplace where everyone had to pass it. That is Paul’s picture of his preaching. He had not offered a spiritual option. He had nailed up a notice saying: the Son of God was executed, and it was for you (1 Corinthians 2:2).

“Before your eyes.” None of them had been at Golgotha, nor had Paul. Preaching that does its work does not merely inform people about the cross; it sets the cross before them until they see it — not theatre or sentiment, but the plain announcement of what happened, so clear that a farmer in Lystra could shut his eyes and see a man on a Roman beam dying in his place.

How it slips. The Galatians were not never told. They were told with total clarity. A clearly seen cross can be talked out of a person’s field of vision without his noticing anything moved. Nobody announced they were abandoning Christ. They were adding a little, adjusting a little, tidying up a gospel that felt untidily free.

A test. Not “do you believe the cross happened?” — almost every reader does. Rather: when you last asked whether God is pleased with you, what did you look at? If the honest answer is your week — your prayers, your temper, your record since Sunday — something has moved into the field of vision, and the notice on the wall has been papered over. Look at Christ crucified again today, and let that answer the question.
verseByVerse.note: “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye. “Publicly portrayed” uses the word for a public notice posted for all to read.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks one question: did you receive the Holy Spirit by keeping the law, or by hearing the gospel and believing? The answer is obvious from their own experience — and it settles everything.

One question is enough. Paul has a whole letter of arguments ready — covenants, chronology, Abraham, Moses, an allegory — and first asks one question, as if to say it suffices. Answer it honestly and the troublers’ programme collapses.

About their biography, not their theology. He doesn’t ask what they believe now — that is what impressive men were renegotiating weekly. He asks what happened then. That is a matter of record, and they were all there.

What happened. A travel-worn stranger walked into their towns and announced a crucified and risen Jew as Lord of the world. Some believed, and God gave them himself. The Spirit came not as a doctrine worked out later but as something they lived through: sins forgiven, a new hunger for God, love for people they had despised, in some cases power (Acts 14:3). Most had not been circumcised, kept a Sabbath, or refused pork. They were uncircumcised pagans who heard and believed, and God moved in.

What was in your hands? The troublers taught that the law completes what faith begins. Paul says: run the tape back. When God gave you the greatest gift there is — his own Spirit — what was in your hands? Nothing. What had you done? Heard and believed. “Hearing with faith” can mean the hearing that consists of faith or the message heard that produces faith; Paul may mean both — a message announced, and a heart that stops arguing and takes it (Romans 10:17). Even the taking is worked by the Spirit received.

A test. When God first became real to you — not your christening or joining a church, but the day it became true rather than inherited — what were you holding? Honestly, nothing. You heard, and something in you gave way. The whole Christian life works out a transaction in which you brought no capital. If anyone tells you your standing now depends on what you bring, he describes a different transaction from the one you made. Thank God for that day, and live today on the same terms.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” The Galatians weren’t abandoning the Spirit; they wanted to “finish properly” by adding law-keeping. Paul calls that foolish. And did they suffer so much for nothing — if indeed it was for nothing?

Begin and finish. “Begun” and “perfected” are a matched pair used of starting and completing a rite. The Galatians weren’t proposing to drop the Spirit. They wanted to complete what the Spirit started. Paul says that is not maturity but madness: you began by God’s power and propose to finish by your own.

What “flesh” means here. Not lust or temper. Circumcision is a cut in literal flesh; the whole programme lands on the body. “Flesh” is the realm of what a human can do, mark, keep and show — religious achievement, visible and yours. Paul isn’t warning them off sin here. He is warning them off religion.

How it happens to good Christians. Almost no believer consciously decides to be justified by works. It happens quietly. You come to Christ with empty hands and are received with joy. Over five years the hands fill: a devotional habit, a serving rota, a standard of speech, a reputation for reliability. None is bad; all may be the Spirit’s fruit. But somewhere the ground of your confidence migrates from Christ’s finished work to the evidence of your progress, and you never notice the day it moved.

A test. Take your worst week — prayed nothing, snapped at everyone, went to church because it was easier than explaining why not. Was God as pleased with you that Sunday as on your best Sunday of the year? If something in you flinches, the flinch is the answer. Not your morals but your foundation has shifted: you have started finishing by the flesh what was begun by the Spirit. Go back to the beginning: come to God today with empty hands (Philippians 1:6).

He can’t finish the sentence. “Did you suffer so many things in vain?” They had paid for their faith; Paul had been stoned at Lystra and left for dead, and the young churches had shared the cost (Acts 14:19–22). Then: “if indeed it was in vain.” The great polemicist breaks off and won’t say it. He raises the danger because they need to feel it, then refuses to close his hand on it. He is furious with them and cannot bear to lose them, and the two are not in tension (4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith— just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who keeps supplying the Spirit and working miracles among them — does he do it because they keep the law, or because they hear and believe? Just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” The Galatians were justified the same way Abraham was.

Present tense. Not “did” God supply but “does” — going on supplying, and working miracles among them now. Whatever the troublers said about their deficient standing, God had not stopped moving among them. The evidence was in the room during the argument.

Lavish provision. “Supplies” comes from the theatre: the wealthy citizen who funded a chorus for the festival, costumes, training and all, at his own expense. It came to mean generous provision by someone under no obligation. That is the verb for how God gives the Spirit. Not wages, but generous underwriting, because he chose to.

Abraham is part of the question. In Greek verse 5 runs straight into verse 6: “…or by hearing with faith — just as Abraham believed God.” Abraham is not a new topic; he is the last clause of the question. What happened in Galatia last year and to Abraham two thousand years earlier is the same transaction: God spoke, a man believed, God credited it as righteousness.

What were these miracles, and do they continue? They were the signs that accompanied the first preaching of the gospel in Galatia; Luke says that at Iconium the Lord “bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands” (Acts 14:3). Paul’s point is not that miracles are normal, but that God gave the Spirit and his powers to people who believed, not to people who kept the law. Continuationists take the present tense here as proof that such works go on in every church. The more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic founding of the churches (2 Cor 12:12; Heb 2:3–4) and have ceased; the Spirit himself, received by faith, remains.

Paul and James on Abraham. James quotes the same verse about Abraham and says he was justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac (Jas 2:21). Genesis 15 gives the verdict; Genesis 22, many years later, shows the faith was real. James speaks of faith vindicated, Paul of faith counted (cf. 2:16).

“Counted.” A bookkeeping word: to post an entry to an account. Abraham had done nothing to earn it. A childless old man under a sky full of stars, told his descendants would be that many, took God at his word — and God wrote “righteous” against his name. Not “improving” or “on probation.” Righteous, in full, that night, before circumcision and before Moriah (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3–5).

Not faith as a cheap work. This doesn’t say Abraham’s faith was so admirable that God accepted it in place of the righteousness he lacked; that would make faith a rather cheap work and put the ground back inside the man. Faith is the empty hand receiving a righteousness that belongs to Another (Philippians 3:9). And if that is how Abraham’s account was settled, nobody after him has a better arrangement. There is no advanced tier. The man at the head of the story got in the way the newest believer in Galatia did. Rest your standing today on that same promise.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So those who believe are Abraham’s true sons. Scripture foresaw God justifying the Gentiles by faith and announced the gospel to Abraham beforehand: “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” Everyone who believes is blessed together with Abraham, the man of faith.

A bombshell. To be a son of Abraham was a legal identity: inside the covenant and promises, traced by blood and marked in the body. A Gentile could enter only by becoming, in effect, a Jew. That was the troublers’ offer, and it looked generous: come the whole way, take the mark, be full sons like us. Paul cuts the ground away: Abraham’s sons are those who share his faith, not his blood. Descent never made a man Abraham’s son in the sense that counted, or Ishmael and Esau would have been in.

The gospel preached to Abraham. “Preached the gospel beforehand” — literally, pre-gospelled him. When God said to a childless Mesopotamian, “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), the gospel was already being announced in seed form. God had the Gentiles in view from the first sentence he spoke to Abraham.

Scripture speaks. Paul says “the Scripture foresaw” and “preached” — a striking way to speak of a book. What Scripture says, God says. When you open your Bible you are not reading about a God who once spoke. You are being spoken to.

The story inside out. The troublers treated Gentile inclusion as a late concession on Jewish terms. Paul says it was the point from the start. The family existed so the blessing could reach everyone else. To demand that a Galatian become a Jew first was to obstruct the very purpose for which Israel was called.

Has the church then replaced Israel? Paul is not saying that the Jewish people have no future, but that Abraham’s true family has always been defined by faith, not blood. Gentiles who believe are added to that family; Jews who believe are its natural members; and unbelieving Jews can be grafted back in (Rom 11:23). Dispensational Christians hold that ethnic Israel remains a separate people of God with its own promises. The more likely reading is that there is one people of God, Abraham’s children by faith, Jew and Gentile together in Christ (3:28–29).

Along with Abraham. Not blessed after him at a lower grade, but along with him. An Anatolian farmer who believed a travelling preacher stands in the same blessing as the patriarch, on the same footing. Many congregations have people who quietly assume they are auxiliary members — the late convert, the one with the disgraceful decade, the one with no Christian family memory, the one who can’t follow the longer arguments. Verse 9 has no room for it. Abraham has believed for four thousand years and is blessed by faith; you believed last March and are blessed by faith. One queue, and everybody got in the same way. If you have been standing at the back, stop.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having proved his case from Abraham, Paul now proves it from the law, and he does it by letting the law speak. Verse 10 says something nobody expects: it is not those who break the law who are under a curse but those who rely on it — the serious, observant, early-rising ones. The proof is Deuteronomy 27:26, the last of the twelve curses Israel answered with its own Amen. Four words carry it: everyone, all things, abide by, and do them. The law is not a pass mark; it is a seamless garment, and it cannot be scored out of a hundred.

Verse 11 states the conclusion as something already plain — no one is justified before God by the law — and grounds it in Habakkuk 2:4, the verse that broke the medieval church open. Verse 12 sets the opposing principle beside it from Leviticus 18:5: the one who does them shall live by them. A thoughtful reader feels the difficulty, since Leviticus is God’s word too. The answer is that the law’s offer was never a bluff; the fault lies not in the law but in the material it works with.

Then v. 13, the summit of the chapter. Christ redeemed us — bought us out of the slave market — from the law’s curse by becoming a curse himself, and the text quoted is Deuteronomy 21:23, the very verse that made a crucified Messiah unthinkable to Saul the Pharisee. Verse 14 gives the purpose twice: so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith — which closes the circle opened by the question in v. 2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

That Christ bore the penalty due to sinners in their place, exhausting the law’s sentence, is not a later development of doctrine but the explicit content of v. 13. The exchange is legally precise. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could fall on those who have no claim to it. This is not sympathetic solidarity — he suffered with us — but substitution: he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

Two guards belong here. First, becoming a curse does not mean the Father ceased to love the Son or turned on him in temper; Jesus said the opposite (John 10:17). The sentence was real and the Father’s delight in the obedient Son was real at the same hour. Second, the Deuteronomy text is about the public display of an already-condemned man, so the tree did not make him cursed — it published the verdict. Saul had read that publication correctly and been wrong about only one thing: whose curse it was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement, a way of securing what faith had begun. Verses 10–12 show that the law has no supplementary setting. It accepts one condition only, and no son of Adam has ever met it, so those who take their stand there have entered a system whose only two verdicts are flawless obedience and curse. Verse 13 names the single exit, and vv. 13–14 together explain how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up holding the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 with their stomach already tight, half expecting confirmation that God is disappointed with them. Read it exactly. The curse is aimed not at their failure but at the thing they were using to cover it. And v. 13 says what became of it: the sentence was carried out, and not on you. Verse 14 adds that the Spirit you already have is the receipt.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who rely on keeping the law are under a curse, for the law itself says, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.” The law demands perfect obedience, and no one gives it.

Not those who break it — those who rely on it. Paul doesn’t say lawbreakers are cursed but those who rely on the law — the serious, observant ones who get up early to keep it. The people who thought the law was their shelter are standing under the one thing it guarantees.

The law’s own closing ceremony. In Deuteronomy 27 Israel stood in two halves on Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim while the covenant was read, and the last of twelve curses is the one Paul quotes (Deuteronomy 27:26). After each, the whole nation answered “Amen.” They ratified the terms themselves.

Four words. “Everyone” — no exemptions. “All things” — the whole code, not a selection. “Abide by” — continuously. “And do them” — performance, not agreement; you can admire a command all your life without obeying it once. The law is not a pass mark but a seamless garment. “Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10). That is not harsh, because the law is not a list of separate regulations but the will of one Person. To break any of it is to say no to him.

A road and a cliff. So the choice is not between an easier and a harder road to God. It is between a road and a cliff. Whoever stands on law-keeping has entered a system with only two verdicts — flawless obedience or curse — and he has already failed and knows it, which is why the law-keeper’s religion is so often anxious under its composure.

For the reader with a tight stomach. You are not a Judaizer. You have just never shaken the sense that God is disappointed with you, and this verse looks like proof. Notice what Paul says and doesn’t. He doesn’t say people who sin are cursed; if he did, there would be no hope for anyone. He says people who rely on law-keeping are cursed, because they chose a standard that will certainly convict them. The curse is not aimed at your failure but at the thing you were trying to use to cover it. Stop using it. In three verses Paul tells you what happened to the curse.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one is justified before God by the law, because “the righteous shall live by faith.” The law works on a different principle: “The one who does them shall live by them.” One way puts the weight on the doer; the other on the One believed. They cannot be blended.

Evident. “It is evident” — plain, already established. The proof is Habakkuk 2:4. Habakkuk watched the Babylonians coming and could not square it with God’s character. The answer he got was not an explanation but a way to survive: the righteous will live — keep standing when everything visible is against him — by faith. Paul takes it as the shape of the whole Christian life (Romans 1:17), Luther took it from Paul, and it broke the medieval church open.

Is God quoted against himself? “The one who does them shall live by them” is Leviticus 18:5, God’s own word. How can Paul use it as the losing side? Because it states the law’s principle truthfully. The law really does promise life to whoever keeps it; that offer was no bluff. The law is “holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). The defect is in the material it works with: the law was “weakened by the flesh” (Romans 8:3) — a sound contract offered to a bankrupt. The terms are excellent. He can’t meet them.

Two kinds of sentence. “Do these things and live” puts the weight on the doer. “The righteous shall live by faith” puts it on the One believed. They are not two ingredients that improve each other but two answers to “who is responsible for my standing before God?” — and the second cancels the first.

Someone did them. Leviticus 18:5 was never revoked. Someone had to do the things and live — and Someone did. One man stood under the law’s own terms and could claim its promise honestly. He earned the life. Then he went where the law had nothing but a curse to give, took the curse, and left the life to us. That is the next verse. Today, stop presenting your doing to God, and trust his.

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith
by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” — as Scripture says, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.” On the cross Christ took the law’s curse in our place, so that it no longer falls on us.

Redeemed. A slave-market word: to buy out, purchase and remove. A real transaction, a real price, a real release. First-century townspeople had watched it happen in the square. And we were bought out not from the law but “from the curse of the law” — verse 10 come home. The sentence over everyone who stood on his own obedience has been carried out, and not on him.

By becoming a curse. Not by pitying us or showing how much God cares. He became the thing itself. And the proof text made every Jew flinch: “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (v. 13, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23; there, “a hanged man is cursed by God”). In Deuteronomy hanging was not the execution. A man was put to death and then his body hung on a tree as a public sign of what he was, and taken down by nightfall. The tree did not make him cursed; it announced it, so everyone passing could read heaven’s verdict.

Saul before a crucifix. For a Pharisee this text was the closing argument against Jesus. Whatever the fishermen claimed, God had published his verdict on a beam outside the city. A crucified Messiah was blasphemy with a scriptural footnote. On the Damascus road the argument didn’t go away; it turned inside out. Saul was right that the tree published a curse. He was wrong about only one thing: whose. “For us.” He was cursed, and not for anything he had done (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24).

A guard for tender consciences. To say Christ became a curse is not to say the Father stopped loving the Son or turned on him in temper. Jesus said the opposite: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life” (John 10:17). The Son was never more precious to the Father than in the hour he bore our sentence, and the sentence was real. Both are true at once.

The exchange. The law had one thing to say to everyone who came to it for a verdict, and it was right to say it. The Son of God took the sentence out of the judge’s mouth before it reached us and carried it out of the city on his own back. The tree designed to publish God’s curse became the place where the curse ran out. When guilt rises over sin you have confessed, look at that tree and say: it fell on him.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was under God’s curse.

parallels.desc: a hanged man is cursed by God

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ took the curse so that the blessing promised to Abraham might come to the Gentiles in him, and so that we might receive the promised Holy Spirit through faith. The cross brings both the blessing and the Spirit to all who believe.

Rescue for something. “So that… so that.” The cross was a rescue from something and for something, and Paul names two results the troublers were quietly denying.

Abraham’s blessing reaches the nations. The line goes back to Genesis 12 and travelled two thousand years, through Isaac, Jacob, a nation, a monarchy and an exile, to arrive in a Galatian town in the hands of people whose grandparents worshipped Zeus. And it arrives “in Christ Jesus” — not because God relaxed the terms or decided circumcision didn’t matter. The troublers wanted Gentiles brought in through the door marked “become a Jew.” God brought them in through the door marked “be in Christ,” the only door there has ever been.

The circle closed. “That we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.” Paul began the chapter asking how they got the Spirit (v. 2). Now he says the cross is why.

The promised Spirit. The Spirit is not a bonus for advanced believers or a second stage for the especially earnest. He is the promise — God himself coming to live in Gentile bodies, as the prophets foretold: “I will put my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27); “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28). The Galatians had him and were being told they lacked something.

Not a lesser version. The commonest Christian discouragement is not doctrinal doubt but the settled suspicion that you received a lesser version of the faith — that others reached a fuller blessing and you didn’t. Verse 14 forecloses it. The blessing of Abraham and the promised Spirit are not two prizes at different levels. They are one gift, bought at one cross, received by one faith. If you are in Christ, you have them. Thank God for the Spirit in you today, and stop looking over your shoulder at others.

What it cost. Nothing was cheapened to let the nations in. The full weight of the law’s sentence fell on the Son outside a city wall, so that a man in Iconium with no covenant, ancestry or merit could be given the Spirit of the living God. He did not lower the terms. He met them, and paid for everyone who never could.

parallels.desc: I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temperature drops and Paul takes the Galatians from Golgotha to a lawyer’s office, calling them brothers again, a warm word breaking through the anger. Verse 15 gives the principle from everyday life: once a covenant or will has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a clause. If that holds for a document drawn up by men who forget things and change their minds, how much more for one God has sworn. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise; they were proposing an amendment, and an amendment is not a modest adjustment but a legal impossibility.

Verse 16 makes the exegetical observation that troubles modern readers: the promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ. Since the word is collective in both Hebrew and Greek, this looks like a trick — until you notice that Paul himself uses it collectively in v. 29. The argument is not about grammar in isolation but about the shape of the history. The promise narrowed at every fork: Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau, Judah, David. It was always funnelling toward one person.

Verse 17 dates it. The law came 430 years after the promise, and the later document cannot cancel the earlier one; the figure follows the Greek Old Testament Paul’s churches used, which counts from Abraham to the exodus. Verse 18 states the either-or underneath: if the inheritance comes by law it no longer comes by promise. These are not two ingredients that improve each other but two answers to the question of who is responsible for my standing, and the second cancels the first.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priority and Indestructibility of the Promise

The covenant of grace — God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s seed — is prior to the Mosaic law and independent of it. This is a foundation of Reformed covenant theology, and vv. 15 and 17 are where Paul argues it. The Mosaic administration does not replace the Abrahamic covenant or amend its terms; it operates within it and serves it for a season, leaving its character as promise untouched.

Verse 16 supplies the reason the promise cannot fail, and it is more than a point of grammar. Had God covenanted with Abraham’s descendants as a body, the covenant would have rested in the hands of a nation that broke every arrangement it was given. He covenanted with one heir who would not break it, and everyone else inherits by being in him. Verse 18 draws the practical edge: God “has given” it, in the perfect tense, and it stands given. A promise whose security is the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything conditioned on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were arguing, in effect, that the later Mosaic legislation modified the conditions of the earlier Abrahamic promise. Verses 15 and 17 show why that is not a theological preference but a legal impossibility, and v. 18 shows what it would cost if it were allowed: not an improved promise but no promise at all.
