Verse 16 removes their last foothold by identifying the heir they were claiming to represent.

Now: The difference v. 18 describes is invisible from the outside. Two Christians can keep the same hours, give the same money and serve on the same rota, one obeying a Father who has already given him the house, the other trying to secure a house he is not sure of. You can tell them apart only when something goes wrong: one fails and runs to his Father, the other fails and hides, because for him the failure has moved the inheritance. Verses 15–18 exist to put every reader in the first category and keep him there.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul uses an everyday example: even a human covenant, once ratified, cannot be cancelled or added to. God’s promises were made to Abraham and to his “offspring” — singular — who is Christ. The promise always had one destination, and it cannot fail because its Heir cannot fail.

A human example, brothers. The temperature drops. He has just been at Golgotha; now he takes them to a lawyer’s office — and calls them “brothers.”

No added clauses. The word means both covenant and last will, and Paul uses the overlap. Once a covenant is sealed and witnessed, no interested party can insert a clause later. If that holds for documents drawn up by forgetful, changeable men, how much more for one God has sworn? The troublers weren’t tearing up the promise to Abraham. They were proposing an amendment: the promise plus a condition. Paul says that is not a modest adjustment but a legal impossibility. It writes a different covenant.

Offspring, singular. Readers frown here. “Offspring” is a collective word, singular in form and plural in meaning, in English, Hebrew and Greek. God promised descendants as numerous as the stars (Genesis 15:5). Is Paul playing with grammar? No — and the proof is v. 29, where he uses the same word collectively of a whole church: “you are Abraham’s offspring.” A man doesn’t build on a word’s singularity and then use it of a crowd unless he knows exactly what the word does.

The promise narrowed. The promise was never handed to Abraham’s descendants as a body. Ishmael was excluded: “through Isaac shall your offspring be named” (Genesis 21:12). Esau was passed over. The line runs to Judah, to David, to David’s house, narrowing at every fork. Read forward, the story is funnelling toward Someone. The singular lets Paul say what the shape of the history always said: one destination, a Person. Genesis hints at it: after the binding of Isaac, God promises that “your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies, and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:17–18) — the pronoun turns singular. Paul reads the Old Testament as the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it (Luke 24:27).

It cannot fail. If the promise was made to Christ, it cannot fail, because its Heir cannot fail. Had God made it with Abraham’s descendants as a body, it would have been in the hands of a nation that broke every covenant it was given. He made it with one Man who would not break it, and everyone else gets in by being in him. Your security is not your record but his.
verseByVerse.note: “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one descendant or many.

parallels.desc: in your offspring shall all the nations be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law, given 430 years after God’s covenant with Abraham, cannot cancel that earlier promise. If the inheritance came by keeping the law, it would no longer come by promise — but God gave it to Abraham by promise.

The older document wins. The promise is older by four centuries, and in any court a later paper cannot cancel an earlier one.

The number. Exodus 12:40 says Israel lived in Egypt 430 years. The Greek Old Testament Paul’s churches used (and the Samaritan text) reads “in Egypt and in Canaan” — 430 years from Abraham to the exodus. Paul counts from the promise to Sinai using the text his readers had. Nothing depends on the exact figure: the promise came first.

Two kinds of thing. “If the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise.” Law and promise are not enemies, but different species. A promise is sworn by one party and received by the other. A law is demanded by one and performed by the other. One inheritance cannot be received on both terms. The moment my performance becomes a condition, the swearing was never the ground.

The house and the tidy room. A father tells his son the house will be his when he dies; it is written, signed and witnessed. Later he says, “And keep your room tidy.” If tidiness is simply how a son given a house behaves in it, nothing has changed. But if tidiness is now the condition of inheriting, the son no longer has a promise. He has a contract, and he will spend his life measuring the floor, never sure.

Obeying God or securing God. That is the difference between a Christian who obeys God and one trying to secure him. From outside they look identical: both up early, both give, both serve. The difference shows when something goes wrong. One fails and runs to his Father. The other fails and hides, because the failure has just moved his inheritance. Which do you do?

“Gave” — and it stands given. The verb is perfect: God has given, and it stands. The deed was signed before Sinai, before there was a law to keep or break, by Someone who does not revise (Romans 4:13–16; Hebrews 6:17–18). Next time you fail, run to him.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt; Paul uses the figure for the long gap between the promise and the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify, cannot give life and cannot amend the promise, the obvious objection has to be faced, and v. 19 faces it: why then the law? Paul answers with three phrases, each of which puts the law in its place without insulting it. It was added because of transgressions — drawing the line that turns vague wrongness into named counts. It was until the offspring should come, with an expiry written into it, not a failure but a term. And it was put in place through angels by an intermediary, which is the sharpest demotion of all.

Verse 20 is the most compressed sentence in the letter, and honest commentators admit that its details are disputed. But the direction is clear from the chain Paul has just counted. A mediator implies two parties; the presence of Moses on the mountain tells you Sinai was a two-sided arrangement that could fail, and it failed at the foot of the mountain. God is one: when he came to Abraham there was no second party, and in Genesis 15 he passed alone between the pieces while Abraham slept through his own covenant.

Verse 21 asks whether the law is therefore contrary to God’s promises and answers with Paul’s strongest negative. They are not rivals but a diagnosis and a cure. He grants freely that if any law could give life, righteousness would have come that way. Verse 22 gives the true verdict: Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, shut in like fish in a net, so that the promise might be given by faith. Verses 23–25 name the jailer’s office — the law was our paidagōgos, the household slave who walked the boy to school until he came of age. Verse 24 says he was doing it so we might be justified by faith, and v. 25 says the arrangement has ended.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Genuine, Severe, Temporary, Fulfilled

Reformed theology has always held to the unity of the covenant of grace across both Testaments while recognising the distinct function of the Mosaic administration within it. Verses 19 and 24 are the classic ground for that. The law was genuinely from God, genuinely binding in its time, and genuinely serving the covenant of grace — but it was designed for a phase and not for the end. Its close as a system of justification is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

Two guards belong with vv. 23–25. It does not follow that God’s moral will has been repealed: Paul will say in 5:14 that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour. What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors. Nor does it follow that Old Testament believers were second-class. They were children in the same family under the care their age required. And v. 22 shows the severity was mercy: the exits were closed so that the one open door would finally be taken.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian reinstated after the child had come of age. Verse 19 answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has expired, v. 20 that the promise never depended on two signatures anyway, and v. 25 that the arrangement is over.

Now: Verses 21–25 meet three readers: the one who assumes his problem is information or willpower, the one who finds that the harder he tries the worse the accounting gets, and the largest group of all — believers who are adults in Christ and still live as if under supervision.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions — to make sin plain — until Christ, the promised Offspring, came. And it was given through angels by a mediator, Moses. The law had a real but limited and temporary job.

The obvious objection. If the law cannot justify, give life, or amend the promise, why give it at all? Was Sinai a mistake? Paul answers in three phrases, each putting the law in its place without insulting it.

“Added because of transgressions.” An addition is not the foundation. Sin was in the world before Sinai, but it was not yet transgression — stepping over a line — because the line had not been drawn. The law drew it, turning the vague human sense that something is wrong into specific counts with names. “I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Romans 7:7). That is a kindness. A man who feels vaguely unwell puts off the doctor for years; a man handed a named diagnosis goes that afternoon. The law is the diagnosis. It doesn’t cause the disease or cure it, and anyone who mistakes the chart for the medicine will die holding it.

“Until the offspring should come.” The law had an expiry written in: not a failure but a term, running until the Offspring of v. 16 arrived. He has come. Insisting on the arrangement after the date is not extra faithfulness; it is standing on the platform arguing about timetables while the train you waited for pulls out.

“Through angels by an intermediary.” Scripture pictures Sinai attended by angels — the Lord coming “from the ten thousands of holy ones” (Deuteronomy 33:2) — and Stephen and Hebrews assume the law came through angels (Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2). Then Moses stood between, because the people begged not to hear God’s voice (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:5). Count the links: God, angels, Moses, Israel. Now the promise: God, Abraham. The law came down a staircase; the promise was handed over directly. To know which is greater, don’t ask which had more smoke on the mountain. Ask how many people God needed between himself and the one he was speaking to.

A test. Let the law do its proper work in you: read the Ten Commandments slowly this week and let them name your sin specifically. Then take the diagnosis to Christ, not back to the chart.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law; Moses was the intermediary.

parallels.desc: I stood between the LORD and you

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“An intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.” Sinai was a two-party arrangement with Moses in the middle, which could fail because Israel could fail. The promise to Abraham was given by God alone, and so it cannot fail.

A famously compressed sentence. Commentators have counted hundreds of readings, and it is honest to admit that. But the direction is clear, because Paul has just counted links in a chain.

Two parties at Sinai. A mediator stands between parties; you don’t need one where there is only one. Moses’ presence on the mountain tells you Sinai was two-sided: God on one side, Israel on the other — “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (Exodus 19:8). Everything depended on both keeping their word, and the ink was barely dry before there was a golden calf.

One party with Abraham. When God came to Abraham there was no second party and no man in the middle. Abraham did not negotiate; he was asleep. In the strangest scene in Genesis, God put him into a deep sleep, and “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces” (Genesis 15:12, 17). In that ceremony both parties normally walked the path between the halves, calling the animals’ fate on whoever broke faith. God walked it alone. He took both halves of the oath on himself, and Abraham slept through his own covenant.

One signature. The contrast is not between a harsh arrangement and a kind one, but between an agreement that can fail because it has two signatures and a promise that cannot fail because it has one — and the One who signed does not have a bad year.

A test. If your standing with God is a two-party arrangement, it is only as secure as your last fortnight; every failure is a breach, and you live in anxious accounting that looks like devotion from outside. If it is a one-party promise, your failures are real and grievous and must be repented of — but they are not renegotiations. Only one name is on the document. Repent today of what you must, without reopening the contract. God walked between the pieces alone under the night sky, and centuries later walked out to a hill alone, and kept his oath (Hebrews 6:13; 2 Timothy 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is the law against God’s promises? “Certainly not!” If any law could give life, righteousness would come by law. But Scripture has locked everything up under sin, so that the promise might be given, through faith in Jesus Christ, to those who believe. God closes every other door so we will take the one he opens.

Diagnosis and cure. Paul has demoted the law three times, so he asks what his opponents would shout. “Certainly not!” Law and promise come from the same God for the same purpose. They are a diagnosis and a cure, and only a fool sets those against each other.

No law can give life. “If a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law.” If any legal code could make a dead man live, God would have used it gladly. The law isn’t blamed for failing at its job; it was never given that job. A speed limit has never made a reckless man careful; it tells him what careful looks like and records that he isn’t. And that measures our condition. If we were only misinformed, instruction would do; if only weak, encouragement. Scripture says we are “dead in the trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1), and nothing you say to a corpse improves it.

Locked in. “The Scripture imprisoned everything under sin.” The verb means shut up together, enclosed — used of fish caught in a net (Luke 5:6). And it is “everything,” the whole realm. Nobody stands outside the net commenting on those inside. And God’s own word turned the key: our confinement is not an accident we can appeal elsewhere. It is published, and it is his.

The mercy in the lock. “So that the promise… might be given to those who believe.” As long as a man thinks there is another way out, he keeps trying doors: being respectable, useful, sincere, spiritual — each holding just enough to keep him busy. God locked every one so we would turn round and see the one door standing open, with a Person’s name on it (Romans 11:32).

For the one at the end of himself. If nothing you can do about yourself seems to work, and the harder you try the worse the accounting gets, don’t read that as God’s absence. It may be his kindness. He is not punishing you with failure; he is closing the exits so you will stop trying to be your own way out and take the one he has provided. Take it today: tell him you are done trying doors, and trust Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before faith came, God’s people were held under the law as under a guardian, until Christ came, so that we might be justified by faith. Now that faith has come, we are no longer under that guardian. The law’s supervising role was real and temporary.

The era of faith. “Before faith came” doesn’t mean no one believed before Christ; Abraham and Habakkuk did. Paul means the age that opened when Christ came and the gospel went to the nations, when faith became the open, announced way in. The Old Testament believer looked down a corridor at a door he could not yet see. We are standing in the room.

The guardian. The law was our paidagōgos. Older versions said “schoolmaster,” which is exactly wrong. He was not the teacher but a household slave — often old, stern, a byword in comic plays for being no fun — put in charge of a boy from about six until he came of age. He walked him to school and home, kept him off the wrong streets, checked his manners, and had a stick and authority to use it. His job was to get the boy to the one who would teach him, and keep him out of trouble on the way.

Three things follow. The guardian was genuinely appointed; the father chose him, and resenting him meant resenting the father’s arrangement. He was genuinely strict; that was the job. And he was genuinely temporary; nobody had a paidagōgos at thirty. Now “we are no longer under a guardian.” The son has come of age. The troublers were going to the grown man in the courtyard and telling him that if he really wanted to please his father, he should send for the old slave and ask to be walked to school.

Two guards. This does not repeal God’s moral will; Paul will spend two chapters telling these people how to live, and says “the whole law is fulfilled in one word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (5:14). What ended is the law as the framework of the relationship — guardianship over minors. Nor were Old Testament believers second-class. They were children in the same family, cared for as their age required (Romans 10:4).

Does the law, then, have any use for Christians? Reformed Christians speak of three uses. The law restrains evil in society; it convicts sinners and drives them to Christ; and it shows believers how to live. What has ended is the law as a guardian, a covenant to live under and a way of being accepted, together with its ceremonial and civil parts. What remains is its moral content, the Ten Commandments summed up in love (5:14; Rom 13:8–10), now written on the heart by the Spirit. Christians are not under the law to be saved, but they are not without law; they are “under the law of Christ” (1 Cor 9:21).

A test. Are you living like a son, or like a boy never told the guardian was dismissed? Many believers are adults in Christ and emotionally still under supervision — measuring the day’s performance, expecting the stick, surprised by kindness. The Father didn’t merely relax the rules. He ended the arrangement and brought the boy into the house as heir. Approach him today as that.
verseByVerse.note: The “guardian” (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a child, took him to school and kept him in line until he came of age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Through faith, all of them are sons of God in Christ Jesus, for all who were baptised into Christ have put him on like a garment. In him the divisions that ruled the ancient world, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, no longer determine anyone’s standing; all are one in Christ. And if they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring and heirs of the promise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a location. He is in Christ, clothed in Christ, and therefore holds the status of the Son. This is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well; the clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer.

Verse 28 is the theological ground of the New Testament’s social revolution. The gospel does not merely change individuals, it creates a community in which the stratifications of the old age no longer determine worth or access. Sincere believers who honour this book read the verse differently when it comes to office and order, some hearing the end of every distinction of role, others holding that Paul speaks of standing here and of roles elsewhere, which is the more natural reading of the whole Pauline corpus. What neither side qualifies is what the verse indisputably says, and it is the larger thing: at the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance of v. 29 there is no smaller share.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jew and Greek was a divide so absolute that a Jew would not enter a Gentile house; slave and free described perhaps a third of a city’s population as property; male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. A saying recorded in later rabbinic sources thanked God for not having been made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Verse 28 takes those three walls and says they do not run through the room. Verses 26–27 explain why: everyone in it is wearing the same garment. Verse 29 tells Gentile believers they are not associate members of a Jewish covenant but full heirs.

Now:Every congregation holds people who have quietly concluded they are second rank. Verse 28 does not offer them a role; it says something better and harder to believe, that Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ Jesus all believers are sons of God through faith. All who were baptised into Christ have “put on Christ” like a garment. Before God, believers are clothed in Christ himself.

Every word aimed. “You” — the uncircumcised Galatians told they weren’t yet full members. “All” — no tiers. “Sons” — not wards or apprentices. “Through faith” — not through the knife. And governing it all, “in Christ Jesus”: the sonship is ours because we are in the Son.

Why “sons.” Paul writes “sons,” not “children,” on purpose, because in that world sons inherited and daughters generally didn’t. The word is about legal status, the standing of the heir. So a woman reading v. 26 isn’t overhearing something addressed to men. She is told she holds the inheritance rights of a firstborn son in God’s household. Two verses later Paul says so outright. It is the most generous word in the sentence.

Put on Christ. The ordinary word for dressing — and it fits the Roman coming-of-age ceremony, when a boy laid aside the child’s striped toga and put on the plain white toga of a man. Paul has just dismissed the guardian; now he hands out the adult garment, and the garment is Christ. So what the Father sees when he looks at a believer is not a person making progress but his Son’s righteousness worn as clothing, covering everything the man is ashamed of and hasn’t yet dealt with (Isaiah 61:10). That is why people who know themselves well can have assurance. The clothing doesn’t fluctuate with the wearer.

Does baptism unite us to Christ? Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read this verse as teaching that baptism is the means by which a person is united to Christ. But the chapter has just said that everything comes through faith (vv. 2, 14, 26), and Paul cannot mean that the water does what faith alone receives. He names baptism because no one in the New Testament imagined a believer who had not been baptized; it is the God-appointed sign and public putting-on of what faith has received. Christians who baptize infants see baptism as the sign of the covenant given, like circumcision, to believers’ children (Col 2:11–12). The more likely reading is that baptism is the sign of faith, given to those who have believed: “as many of you as were baptized” are those who, through faith, are sons of God (v. 26).

A test. There is no better-dressed Christian in your congregation than you. The most disciplined believer you know is wearing exactly what you are wearing, and neither of you made it or paid for it (Romans 13:14). When you feel shabby before God this week, remember whose clothes you are in.

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” In their standing before God and their share in the inheritance, every believer is equal. Differences remain, but they are no longer measures of worth or conditions of access.

The walls of the ancient world. These pairs were the load-bearing walls of that world. Jew and Greek: a religious divide so absolute that a Jew would not enter a Gentile house. Slave and free: the economic order, in cities where a large share of the population were property. Male and female: whose testimony counted in court. A saying in later rabbinic sources, probably reflecting older sentiment, thanked God for not being made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Paul says that in Christ these walls do not run through the room.

“No male and female.” The first two pairs are “neither… nor”; the third changes to “no male and female” — the exact Greek of Genesis 1:27, “male and female he created them.” Paul reaches past the social order to creation: even the deepest distinction God made in humanity does not decide your standing in Christ.

What is levelled. The context is who is Abraham’s son, who is justified, who is clothed in Christ, who inherits. On that ground the walls are gone. There is not a Jewish justification and a Gentile one, a free man’s adoption and a slave’s, a fuller portion for a husband and a lesser one for his wife. One Christ, one righteousness, one inheritance, and every believer holds all of it. Differences themselves remain: Paul stays a Jew; Onesimus remains legally a slave while Paul works on Philemon to change it; men and women remain men and women. What has gone is difference as a measure of worth and a condition of access.

Does it erase all difference of role? Egalitarian Christians argue that if there is no male and female in Christ, there can be no difference of role in the church or the home; they see the verse as the principle and the restrictions elsewhere as temporary concessions to Paul’s culture. But Paul is speaking here of who belongs to Christ and inherits the promise (v. 29), and in the same period he taught that husbands and wives have different callings (Eph 5:22–33; Col 3:18–19) and that elders should be men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:2), grounding this in creation, not in culture. Slavery is no exception: Paul gave instructions to slaves while sowing the seeds of their freedom (Philemon), but he never grounded slavery in creation. The more likely reading is that men and women are equal heirs in Christ, while God still gives them different roles. Both sides confess what the verse plainly says: at the foot of the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance no smaller share.

For the second rank. Every congregation has people who have concluded they are second rank — the woman talked past in every church she has attended, the man whose accent, job or prison record marks him out, the family never asked to host anything, the convert whose parents aren’t believers and who feels the room close slightly at testimony time. Verse 28 doesn’t offer them a role. It says something better: you are not on the edge of this. Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building than the one he has given you. And if you are in no danger of feeling second rank, go and sit with someone who is this Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.” The promise was made to Christ; everyone who belongs to Christ is in him, and so inherits everything promised.

One question. The promise was made to the Offspring, who is Christ (v. 16). So everything depends on one question: are you his? If so, you are inside the One to whom everything was promised, and it is all yours. The requirements were never lowered. Every one was met by one Man, and you are in him.

Does the church replace Israel? Does this mean that the church replaces Israel, and that the promises of land and nation are now void? Paul says that all who are Christ’s are Abraham’s heirs, so the promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared by everyone in him, Jew and Gentile alike. That is not a rejection of the Jewish people; Paul himself was one, and he insists, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Rom 11:1). Dispensational Christians hold that the land and nation promises remain for ethnic Israel; covenantal premillennialists expect a future earthly fulfilment as well. The more likely reading is that the promise to Abraham was always larger than a strip of land: he would be “heir of the world” (Rom 4:13), and the inheritance is the renewed creation, which belongs to all who are Christ’s.

Heirs. An heir hasn’t merely been given a gift; he has been given a standing, and the estate follows from it. He doesn’t earn it, can’t be dismissed from it, and doesn’t receive it for being useful. He receives it because of who he is in the family. That is why no one in the New Testament is told to work at becoming an heir (Romans 8:16–17).

What is inherited. Scripture is not vague, and our vagueness about the future is a loss, not piety. God himself as your portion: “I am your shield; your reward shall be very great” (Genesis 15:1). A body raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). A world put right and handed over: “the meek… shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5; Romans 8:17–21). A face to see — what Moses asked for and was not given: “they will see his face” (Revelation 22:4; 1 John 3:2). And real work in a real kingdom (Luke 19:17). That stands to the account of the Galatian farmer who believed a travelling preacher, and to yours.

Now. Paul doesn’t say you may one day become an heir if things go well. You are — now, while the estate is unseen and your life mostly contradicts it. Everything else you own can be taken by a diagnosis, a market, a war or time. An inheritance held in Christ has none of those exposures, because its security is his grip, not yours.

A test. Write down three things you are promised as Christ’s heir, from the verses above, and read them the next time you feel poor before God. God swore a promise to one man under a night sky, kept it through centuries of a people who broke every term, narrowed it to one Offspring who carried the curse out of the city, and paid it to everyone with no claim on it. Nothing was cheapened, nothing waived, nothing failed.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.<sup>2</sup>Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?<sup>3</sup>Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?<sup>4</sup>Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?<sup>5</sup>Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—<sup>6</sup>just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?<sup>7</sup>Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham.<sup>8</sup>And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”<sup>9</sup>So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.<sup>10</sup>For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”<sup>11</sup>Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”<sup>12</sup>But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”<sup>13</sup>Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—<sup>14</sup>so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.<sup>15</sup>To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified.<sup>16</sup>Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.<sup>17</sup>This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void.<sup>18</sup>For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.<sup>19</sup>Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.<sup>20</sup>Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.<sup>21</sup>Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law.<sup>22</sup>But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.<sup>23</sup>Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed.<sup>24</sup>So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.<sup>25</sup>But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,<sup>26</sup>for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith.<sup>27</sup>For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.<sup>28</sup>There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.<sup>29</sup>And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the emotional and theological apex of the letter’s central argument. Paul has shown that the law functions as a guardian for children; now he shows what the alternative is: full sonship, the Spirit of the Son, and the cry of “Abba! Father!” from the depths of the adopted heart. The contrast is not merely between two systems but between two existences — the existence of the slave who must perform, and the existence of the son who simply belongs.

The chapter’s opening argument (vv. 1–7) draws on the legal reality of an heir who is underage: he possesses everything but controls nothing, lives under guardians and managers until the time set by the father. Israel under the law was in this condition — heirs of the promise but living under the law’s custody until “the fullness of time.” Then God acted: he sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And confirmation: he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” — the most intimate address to God in all of Scripture, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), now placed on the lips of every adopted child of God.

The chapter then turns to a personal appeal (vv. 12–20) of remarkable emotional intensity — Paul reminding the Galatians of how they received him when he first came to them, sick and in need, and how they would have plucked out their eyes for him. His anguish over their drift is the anguish of a parent whose children are being led away: “for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!” Finally, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31) makes the theological point in narrative form: the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and only the children of the free woman — the children of promise, of grace, of the Spirit — are the true heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul illustrates with an heir who is still a child: though he owns the estate, he is no better off than a slave, living under guardians until the time his father has set. In the same way, we were enslaved to the basic principles of this world. But when the appointed time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman and born under the law, to redeem those under the law so that we might be adopted as sons. And because they are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying out “Abba! Father!” So they are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs through God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Double Sending of Son and Spirit

Verses 4–6 are among the most trinitarian sentences Paul ever wrote. The Father sends the Son; the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two missions are distinct and inseparable: the Son accomplishes redemption and adoption as objective legal realities outside us, and the Spirit applies them within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls him by name.

Adoption (huiothesia) is the doctrine this chapter states most clearly, and it goes beyond forgiveness. In Roman practice the adopted son took the father’s name, inherited on the same footing as any natural son, and, in some forms of Roman adoption, found his former obligations extinguished; the act was witnessed and irreversible, because what had changed was not his conduct but his family. Verse 7 draws the conclusion in three words — no longer, son, heir — and adds through God, so that nobody imagines an inheritance of this size arriving any other way. J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe. They had the Spirit, they had cried Abba, they were heirs. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and Paul’s answer in vv. 1–3 is to show them what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians, the managers, and a calendar. A son does not earn his way into a family he is already in.

Now:The test v. 3 suggests catches good practices rather than bad ones, and v. 6 answers the reader who does not feel like a son: the Spirit is sent because you are one, so the feeling is the consequence of the status and never the cause of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An heir who is still a child, though he legally owns everything, lives no differently from a slave. He is under guardians and managers until the date his father has set. God’s people before Christ were like that: true heirs, not yet able to enjoy what was theirs.

Owner and slave at once. In law he owns the land, house, animals and servants. In practice it makes no difference, because he is seven. He can’t sell a field or give an order anyone must obey. He eats what he’s given and goes where he’s taken. Watch him through the day and you couldn’t tell him from the boy who carries the water.

Old Testament believers. Were believers before Christ saved? Yes, genuinely, by faith, on the same ground as we are. Then why does the New Testament speak of their condition as bondage? Because ownership and enjoyment differ. They held title deeds to promises they could not yet handle. Abraham was “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13) and died having bought only one field, to bury his wife (Genesis 23).

Guardians and managers. One had authority over the boy’s person, the other ran the property. Both were servants, both had more practical power than the owner — and both held it only “until the date set by his father.” Customs varied, but every version shared one feature: the boy didn’t choose the day, nor the guardians. The father named it, and when it came, it came.

For the one frustrated about timing. Much Christian frustration is not doubt but timing: the prayer unanswered for eleven years; the change in yourself you keep asking for and not receiving; the season that has gone on so long you’ve stopped expecting it to lift. Verse 2 doesn’t promise the date is soon. It says there is one, that it isn’t arbitrary, and that a Father fixed it, not the guardians who currently seem to be running your life. The child has no say in the calendar and no reason to fear it. Bring your “how long?” to your Father today, and leave the date with him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way, before Christ came, all of us — Jews and Gentiles — were like children enslaved to “the elementary principles of the world.” Whatever God-given or man-made thing is made the ground of our standing before God becomes a master that enslaves.

“We.” Paul speaks to a mixed church and includes himself, the Pharisee, in the same sentence as men who grew up sacrificing to Cybele.

A disputed phrase. “Elementary principles” translates stoicheia, things in a row — the alphabet, the ABCs, basic building blocks. Some take it as the elementary stage of religion, rudiments God gave the world before the Son came; going back to them now is an adult sounding out letters. Others hear something darker, since Paul says “enslaved,” and the word was used of the spiritual powers thought to stand behind the nations and their calendars; going back to law-keeping is then a return to territory that has an occupant (cf. Colossians 2:8, 20). Most readers combine the two, and Paul’s argument doesn’t depend on choosing. Two things are certain: the Gentiles were under them before they knew God, and the troublers would put the Galatians back under them.

Moses and Cybele in one drawer. That is what makes verse 3 devastating. Paul is not saying Moses and pagan worship are morally equivalent; he calls the law holy. He is speaking of function. Take any good, God-given thing — Sabbath, law, sacraments, a doctrinal system, a discipline of prayer — and make it what secures your standing with God, and it will do to you what an idol does. It will demand, never say “enough,” and you will serve it.

A test. Take the most valued religious habit in your life — daily reading, giving, fasting, service — and imagine dropping it for a fortnight, not through rebellion but illness. What rises in you: disappointment or dread? Disappointment is a son who has missed his father’s company. Dread is a slave who has missed a quota. The habit is identical; the relationship isn’t. If you find dread, keep the habit — and remind yourself whose son you are.
verseByVerse.note: The “elementary principles” may mean the basic rules of religion, or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.” At the moment the Father chose, the eternal Son became fully human and lived under the law, to buy us out of its bondage and make us God’s children.

The fullness of time. The moment the vessel was full to the brim, not early or late. Why then, in an obscure province under Augustus? Some of the answer is visible: Roman roads running the length of the world and a Roman peace to walk them; one language a Galatian, Roman and Alexandrian could all read; synagogues in every major city with God-fearing Gentiles already attached; and a civilisation whose confidence in its gods had drained away. But the deeper answer is in the sentence: it was “the date set by his father” (v. 2). History was waiting for a Father to say “now.”

Every clause precise. “God sent forth his Son” — one already his Son, there to be sent. “Born of woman” — the Hebrew way of saying human, mortal, of our stock (Job 14:1). He didn’t appear in the world; he was carried in it, delivered, fed at a human breast. “Born under the law” — inside the jurisdiction that had us condemned: circumcised on the eighth day, presented with the poor family’s two birds, taken to Jerusalem at twelve (Luke 2:21–24, 41–42), keeping every clause of the code that was killing us.

“Of woman,” not “of a virgin”? Some argue Paul knew nothing of the virgin birth. That is more weight than the sentence bears. Paul isn’t writing about how Jesus was conceived but about which side of the counter he stood on, pressing him further into our condition. “Born of woman” is the last thing you’d expect from someone who thought the Son merely appeared human. And Luke, who travelled with Paul, records the annunciation in detail (Luke 1:26–38).

Redeemed, then adopted. “To redeem” is the slave-market word of 3:13: to buy out. Then more than release: adoption. In Roman practice a man without a suitable heir took a young man, often adult, into his family by a formal legal act before witnesses. From then on he bore the new father’s name and inherited as any natural son; in some forms his old obligations were cancelled. The act could not be reversed, and no later misbehaviour undid it, because what changed was not his conduct but his family.

New birth and adoption. New birth makes someone a child of God by an inward act — a heart made alive, so he begins to want what he never wanted (John 1:12–13). Adoption is an outward legal act: a standing conferred, a name given, an inheritance settled, done by Someone else. That is why assurance is not finally a matter of examining your feelings. On days when inward evidence is hard to find, the outward act stands where it stood, because it was never yours to perform.

A family, not just a rescue. Redemption alone would be extraordinary: the slave bought out of the market and freed at the gate — owing everything, with nowhere to go. God didn’t stop at the gate. He bought the slave, cancelled the debt, gave him his name, and walked him into the house as a son with the firstborn’s inheritance (Romans 8:15). When you pray today, pray as a son in the house, not a freed slave at the gate.

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God. The Spirit’s cry is the result of being a son, not the way to become one.

Status first, experience second. “Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit.” Not: cry Abba hard enough and you will become a son; not: work up the feeling and God will respond. Sonship comes first, established by Christ’s redemption (v. 5); the Spirit is sent because of it. So when the feeling is absent — as it is for many believers for long stretches, in illness, depression, grief, or plain tiredness — nothing has happened to the sonship. A son asleep in bed is as much his father’s son as one laughing at the table.

The Spirit of his Son. Named here as the Son’s own Spirit, because what he brings into your heart is the Son’s relationship with the Father. You aren’t given a new arrangement of your own; you are brought inside his.

Abba. It is often said this is baby-talk, “Daddy.” It isn’t; grown men used it of their fathers all their lives. But the truth is no less moving: it was the ordinary, intimate word a family used inside the house — not the formal word for the deity — the word a son used turning in the doorway. Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and the Spirit puts it in your mouth.

Who cries? Here the Spirit cries; in Romans, “we cry” (Romans 8:15). Both are true: a Christian’s prayer is the Spirit of God praying in him. So the man who says he can’t pray — three words and he dries up, feels nothing, is ashamed of how thin it sounds — is describing the outside of something. The cry that reaches the Father is the Son’s Spirit, and he is not thin. Pray today anyway, beginning with “Father.”

“You” — singular. All letter long Paul has said “you” plural; here he narrows: “you are no longer a slave, but a son.” He wants one person to hear it. Carry three words this week: “no longer” — a door has shut behind you; slavery is your history, not your condition. “Son” — the status given. “Heir” — “through God,” because an inheritance this size could come no other way (Romans 8:15–17; Ephesians 1:5).
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before they knew God, the Galatians were enslaved to beings that are not really gods. Now that they know God, or rather are known by him, how can they turn back to those weak and worthless principles and want to be enslaved again, observing special days and seasons? Paul fears his labour among them was wasted. He pleads with them to become like him, as he became like them. He recalls how they welcomed him when he first preached to them because of a bodily illness, treating him like an angel of God, even like Christ, and would have torn out their eyes for him. Has he become their enemy by telling the truth? The rivals court them for selfish ends. Paul, like a mother in labour again until Christ is formed in them, wishes he could be with them, because he is at a loss about them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Symmetry of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

Paul’s equation in vv. 8–10 of Judaizing observance with the pagan calendar the Galatians had left is about function, not moral equivalence: any God-given thing made the ground of acceptance will behave like an idol. Reformed theology has always held that moralism is not a minor error but a rival gospel that produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 also contains one of Paul’s clearest incidental statements of election, dropped in as a pastoral correction rather than a seminar topic. To be known by God is not for God to learn facts but for God to set his love on a person and claim him (Jer. 1:5). And v. 19 supplies the only metric for ministry the New Testament finally accepts: not attendance, giving or doctrinal precision, but Christ formed — morphōthē, taking shape from within, the word used of a child forming in the womb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly in vv. 14–15 and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain the mechanism. The Judaizers courted them, flattered them, and held the door a few inches short of open. Verse 20 shows what Paul wanted instead: not their allegiance to him but Christ formed in them, which is why he would rather have been in the room than winning on paper.

Now:Verse 10 raises the question every honest reader asks about Christmas, Easter and Sunday, and Paul answers it himself in Romans 14:5–6: what he attacks here is not the observance but the ground. Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy, and v. 13 belongs to the reader whose life has been rerouted by his body.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the Galatians knew God, they were enslaved to beings that are not truly gods. Now that they know God — or rather are known by God — how can they turn back to those weak and worthless elementary principles and want to be slaves again?

Religious and enslaved. These were not atheists. Galatia was crowded with religion — the mother goddess with ecstatic priests, the imperial cult with temples in every colony, household shrines, local shrines at springs. They had been intensely religious and enslaved at once, a combination most people assume impossible. “By nature are not gods”: nothing was behind the statues, yet the whole system of fear and appeasement had owned them.

Are idols nothing, or demons? Both, in different senses. The gods the idols represent do not exist as gods; they are by nature not gods. But Paul says elsewhere that “what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons” (1 Cor 10:20). Behind the empty idol stand real spiritual powers who use the worship of nothing to enslave people (cf. v. 3).

“Or rather to be known by God.” Paul starts, “now that you have come to know God,” and corrects himself mid-sentence. The first phrasing puts the Galatians in the active seat, as though their discovery were the decisive event. He can’t let that stand even for a clause. Yes, they know God now, and it is the sweetest thing about them. But the decisive verb is God’s: they were known — sought, chosen and drawn before they turned a thought toward him.

What “known” means. Not that God learned facts about them. In Scripture, for God to know someone is to set his love on him and claim him: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jer. 1:5). Some read “known by God” as meaning only that God recognised or foresaw their faith. But when Scripture says God knows a people, it means he has set his love on them: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2). Paul corrects himself on purpose: the Galatians came to know God because God first knew them.

Ask the assurance question the right way round. If your Christian life began with you, it can be ended by you, and every wobble threatens it. If it began with God knowing you, then what lies under your faith is not your grip. Don’t ask “do I know God well enough?” — nobody does. Ask “does God know me?” And the evidence that he does is that you are asking at all. Nobody who has not been sought goes looking.

Wanting the chains. “Weak and worthless” — unable to deliver what they demand, beggarly, with nothing in the account. And “whose slaves you want to be.” Paul won’t let them call this mere pressure. Somewhere they wanted it. That is the strangest thing about religious bondage: a system that tells you exactly what to do and where you stand is restful in a way grace at first is not. Grace gives you nothing to hold. Slavery hands you a list. If you find yourself wanting the list, take that longing to the God who knows you.

parallels.desc: no gods, but the work of men’s hands

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galatians are now observing “days and months and seasons and years” — the Jewish religious calendar — as part of their standing with God. Paul fears his work among them may have been wasted. The issue is not keeping special days, but treating them as necessary for acceptance.

No verb of judgment. Paul simply reports what they do, and the exclamation carries the weight. He was raised on that calendar — Sabbaths, new moons, festivals like Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, sabbatical years — God-given in the book he believed to be God’s word, now kept by Gentile converts wanting to please God. And he can hardly speak.

Christmas, Easter, Sunday? Is a church calendar a return to bondage? No, and Paul settles it. To Rome he writes: “One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” — and neither is to despise the other, because both do it “in honor of the Lord” (Romans 14:5–6). He allows both in one congregation.

And what of the weekly Sabbath? Many Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds as the Lord’s Day, and that Paul is condemning only Jewish ceremonial days. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is among the days in view, part of the shadow fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17), so that no day binds the conscience. Gathering on the first day to worship the risen Christ is a good and ancient practice; what Paul forbids is treating any day as part of the ground of our acceptance.

The ground, not the observance. The Galatians weren’t marking Passover in gratitude; they were taking on the calendar as what would complete their standing, on the advice of men who said their faith was insufficient without it. The same act can be worship or slavery depending on what it is asked to do.

Everyone has a calendar. Sunday attendance, daily reading, the annual conference, Lent, family devotions. All good; all potentially either. A test this week: when you keep it, is it gratitude? When you miss it, is the loss the fellowship — or the credit? A Christian who misses church with flu and feels sorrow is worshipping. One who misses it and feels exposed is observing days.

A frightened father. “I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.” No thunder now. The man issuing anathemas admits fear, to their faces, which disarms more than any warning. He has years in these towns — the stoning, the nights teaching — and sees it all going.

Does Paul fear that the Galatians are lost? He fears for them; he does not pronounce on them. Some of those in the churches may never have been truly converted, and Paul knows that a church can contain both. But he writes to them as his “little children” (v. 19), and his fear is the anguish of a father, the same warning that God uses to keep his people from falling away (cf. 5:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begs the Galatians to become like him, because he became like them: he laid down his Jewish advantages to stand with Gentiles on Christ alone; they must not now take up what he put down. And they have not wronged him — this is not a personal grievance.

Begging. “Brothers, I entreat you” — the verb for begging, used when a man has run out of arguments and is simply asking.

“I have become as you are.” Paul was a Jew of impeccable pedigree — “circumcised on the eighth day… of the tribe of Benjamin… a Pharisee” (Philippians 3:5). He had by birth every marker the troublers were selling, and he laid them down. He lived among Gentiles as they lived, ate at their tables, sat loose to the calendar, and refused to make his heritage the ground of anything. In his own people’s eyes he became a man with no standing. So: “become as I am.” I gave up my law-keeping to stand where you stand, on Christ alone. Don’t walk into the room I walked out of.

What it cost him. To Philippi he listed what he had laid down — pedigree, tribe, blamelessness under the law — and said he counted it “as rubbish” for “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:7–8). The word is what you throw out. He had held the whole hand the troublers were dealing and thrown it in the fire, and he begs the Galatians not to scrabble for it.

A question for you. Some believers have never had to give anything up for Christ. But most carry something they have never considered laying down: a family standing, a competence they are known for, a record of respectability, a theological rigour that has become an identity. None is wrong to have. Every one is fatal to hold as the thing that makes you acceptable. Find out which you are doing by asking what it would take from you if it were gone.

“You did me no wrong.” He is answering something. The Galatians might think a furious man must have a personal injury somewhere. Paul removes that possibility, so it can’t be used to explain away what he says. That is worth copying when you must say a hard thing to someone you love. The temptation is to let your hurt do the work, because a wound wins arguments. Paul refuses the advantage and clears his grievance out of the way first, so they have nothing to react to but the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul first preached in Galatia because he was ill. Though his condition was hard to look at, the Galatians did not despise him; they welcomed him as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus himself. God used Paul’s illness to bring them the gospel.

The gospel came because he was ill. Paul hadn’t planned to preach there. Something happened to his body that stopped or diverted him, and while in that condition he preached, and churches were born.

What was the ailment? We don’t know, and that is better than a confident guess. Some suggest malaria from the coastal lowlands, driving him up to the plateau where these towns are. Some suggest an eye disease, given the gouged-out eyes of v. 15 and the large letters of 6:11. Others think of the thorn in the flesh (2 Corinthians 12:7). Paul’s silence means no sick Christian can be told his affliction isn’t the kind God uses.

The illness was the mechanism. Not the obstacle to the mission but how it happened. That is a hard providence to receive while it is happening; nobody lying in a fever in a foreign town is thinking about the churches that will come of it. Paul saw it afterwards, which is usually how it works. Joseph in the pit, Jeremiah in the cistern, John on Patmos, Paul in chains writing the prison letters: God’s habit of building his church out of interrupted plans is nearly the rule. If your life has been rerouted by your body, ask God to show you, in time, what he is building.

“You did not spit.” “Did not scorn or despise me” — the second verb literally means “you did not spit.” Meeting someone visibly diseased, people spat to ward off contagion and the evil eye assumed to be behind it. Set that beside 3:1, “Who has bewitched you?” — the evil eye again. The Galatians once refused to treat a sick preacher as a man under a curse. Now someone has looked at them and they are enchanted. Paul reminds them what they used to be like.

As Christ Jesus. They took a sick, unimpressive, perhaps repellent stranger and received him “as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus” — which, in the only sense that matters, he had come to town. A test: how do you receive the unimpressive messenger, the sick or awkward believer through whom God speaks? Receive them this week as you would receive Christ (Matthew 25:40).
verseByVerse.note: We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where has the Galatians’ joy gone? Once they would have torn out their own eyes and given them to Paul. Has he now become their enemy for telling them the truth? Losing the gospel shows first as lost gladness, and the truth-teller becomes the opponent.

Blessedness. The word behind the Beatitudes — the happiness of people who know they have been given everything. Paul isn’t asking where their doctrine went but where their joy went. That is diagnostic. Legalism rarely announces itself by error first. It shows as a change of atmosphere: the doctrine broadly right, the meetings running, the language Christian — and the gladness gone, replaced by an earnest, watchful, anxious carefulness everyone mistakes for seriousness. To know whether a church has drifted, don’t start with its confession. Start with whether anyone in it looks relieved.

Their eyes. “You would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me” — perhaps a proverb for giving what you value most, perhaps pointing at his actual condition. Either way, there was nothing they wouldn’t have given him.

“Your enemy by telling you the truth?” One of the loneliest sentences in the New Testament. “Telling the truth” is the root of “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). Paul hasn’t changed; he says what he always said. What changed is what they will hear, and so the man who loves them most is filed as the opposition. Every pastor reaches this verse, and so does every Christian who has told a friend something true: the particular grief of being reclassified by people you helped, watching it happen in their faces.

Two things to hold. Being treated as the enemy is not proof you were wrong; the letter assumes Paul is right and unwelcome at once. Nor is it proof you were right; some are treated as enemies because they told the truth, some because they enjoyed telling it. The test is what Paul does next: he doesn’t withdraw or harden. Within three verses he calls them “my little children” and speaks of labour pains. Truth-telling that has stopped hurting the teller has usually stopped being love (Proverbs 27:6). If you have had to tell someone a hard truth, keep loving them now.

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false teachers court the Galatians, but for a bad purpose: they want to shut them out so that the Galatians will court them in return. Being sought after is good when it is for a good purpose — and when it lasts even when the person is absent.

A suitor. “Make much of you” is the word for courting, paying ardent attention. The troublers weren’t bullying the Galatians; they were flattering them, singling them out, making them feel worth a long journey and a personal interest.

The hook. “They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them.” The courting is bait; the shutting out is the hook. Draw someone close enough to feel belonging, then hold the door a few inches short of open, so belonging is always nearly his and never quite. He will work harder and harder for approval that is always about to be granted, and end up defining himself by the people withholding it.

Spiritual manipulation. It doesn’t require a heretic. It happens wherever a leader’s significance depends on being needed, and it can be sincere. The signs are consistent: unusual attention early; a suggestion that you are seen more clearly here than anywhere else; a group with an inside; a standard you are always approaching; and a quiet impression that leaving would be betrayal rather than departure. If you recognise that pattern in a room you are sitting in, this verse is for you. Talk to a wise believer outside that circle.

Good zeal. Paul isn’t sour about affection. “It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present.” Two marks of healthy zeal. Purpose: what do they want you for? A teacher who wants Christ formed in you is delighted when you grow past needing him. One who wants you to make much of him finds your independence threatening and says so in spiritual language. Durability: attention switched on in the room and off outside it was never about you. The love worth having keeps working when the person is far away — exactly what Paul is doing as he writes, absent, unpopular, still labouring over them.

A test for leaders. If you lead others, are you glad when they need you less? Aim to form Christ in them, not dependence on you.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“My little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!” Paul longs to be with them and speak more gently, because he is at a loss about them. The goal of all ministry is Christ taking shape in people.

A parent. The anger drops out, and what is left is a parent. Paul uses this tender address — “my little children” — nowhere else, and at the point where he has least reason to be tender.

A mother in labour. Elsewhere he calls himself the churches’ father (1 Corinthians 4:15). Here he is their mother, in labour — the word for birth pangs. He went through it once to bring them to birth; now he goes through it again. That is not a picturesque way of saying he is concerned. It means he is being torn.

“Until Christ is formed in you.” Not until they come back to him, admit he was right, or repudiate his opponents. The verb is from the root of “transformed” (Romans 12:2) and “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29): something taking its proper shape from inside, like a child forming in the womb. Paul is in labour, and the child is Christ taking shape in them.

The measure of ministry. Almost everything else that gets measured is easier: attendance, giving, doctrinal precision. A congregation can be strong in all of them while Christ is no more formed in them than a decade ago. Paul’s measure is simple and searching: do these people look more like Jesus than they did? A ministry producing admirers, partisans, or well-informed critics of other churches has produced something — but not this. Ask that question of your own church, and of yourself, this year.

Wishing he could change his tone. He knows how the letter sounds. He is not withdrawing the anathemas, but would give much to be in the room, because a letter can’t modulate and a voice can. He wants to say the same words with his face visible.

“I am perplexed about you.” At a loss, with no way through. The apostle who has just settled justification for the whole church doesn’t know what to do about these particular people. That is a mercy for anyone praying for someone who has drifted. Certainty about the truth and bewilderment about a person are not incompatible. Paul had both. Keep praying for them in your bewilderment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — Hagar and Sarah: Two Covenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the story of Abraham’s two sons, one by the slave woman Hagar, born in the ordinary way, and one by the free woman Sarah, born by promise. He reads them as two covenants: Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery with her children; Sarah stands for the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother, as Isaiah promised the barren woman many children. Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise. As the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit then, so it is now. Scripture says to drive out the slave woman and her son, so believers are children not of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.theology:
Typology, and Why the Two Covenants Cannot Share a House

Verse 24 is not allegory in the Alexandrian sense that dissolves history. Paul’s premise is that it is written that Abraham had two sons; he treats the mothers, the statuses and the manner of each birth as facts. He is saying the history happened and was designed to carry a meaning the coming of Christ has made visible — which is what the risen Christ himself did on the Emmaus road (Lk. 24:27). If God governs history, a pattern in a true story is not imposed by the reader; it is put there by the author.

Verses 24–25 supply the test that governs the whole section: what a covenant produces tells you what kind of covenant it is. Sinai was genuinely from God and still bore children for slavery, because that was its office. And v. 30 states the reason a mixture is impossible. Add merit to grace and the result is not a moderate position but merit, since the moment performance is part of the ground the whole weight has moved onto it. Two guards belong with v. 30: Paul casts out a system, not persons — he is in labour pains for the people who hold it — and Genesis itself has God hearing Ishmael in the desert and being with him as he grew (Gen. 21:17–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers presented themselves as the true heirs of Abraham. Verse 22 shows that blood was never the mechanism, v. 23 that the difference lay in how each son came to exist, and vv. 24–25 place the Jerusalem establishment on the slave woman’s side. Verse 29 then explains why religious men were persecuting a Gentile church: a man who has spent his life earning his standing cannot hear that a farmer who believed last month is equally accepted, because it writes off the investment. The elder brother of Luke 15:29–30 says nothing untrue about himself and is furious.

Now:Verse 23 finds most readers before the Judaizers do: the situation you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long is Hagar’s tent. And v. 29 is a warning before it is a comfort: watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul turns to those who want to be under the law: do they actually listen to the law? Abraham had two sons — Ishmael, by the slave woman Hagar, born “according to the flesh”; and Isaac, by the free woman Sarah, born “through promise.” The difference is between what human ability arranges and what only God gives.

Read your own book. “You who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?” — the law here meaning the five books of Moses. Paul answers the law-keepers from the story of the man they claim as father.

Blood was never the mechanism. Abraham had two sons. Physical descent can’t be the qualification, because Ishmael had it. He was Abraham’s son, circumcised at thirteen by Abraham’s own hand (Genesis 17:23), and outside the covenant line. The family tree proves it before you leave Genesis.

How each son came to be. Ishmael came from a plan. God promised Abraham a son; ten years passed (Genesis 16:3); Sarah did the arithmetic on her own body, concluded God needed help, and offered her slave. It was legal, customary, and it worked — a healthy boy, as intended. That is “according to the flesh”: not immorality but competence — human ability doing what it can on God’s behalf because waiting had become unbearable. Isaac came from nothing. Sarah was ninety, past every natural possibility, and had laughed at the announcement (Genesis 18:12). There was no mechanism — a promise, then a baby, and nothing between that anyone could take credit for (Genesis 21:1–3).

Assisting the promise. Two ways of getting a result: what a capable person can arrange, and what only God can give. Everyone believes God can save; the live question is whether he needs help. The Galatians weren’t planning to abandon Christ any more than Abraham planned to abandon the promise. They proposed to assist it.

Hagar’s tent. The instinct is universal and usually looks like responsibility. The thing you have decided you must arrange because God is taking too long — the situation you are managing, the outcome you are engineering, the good end pursued by means you’d rather not examine — that is Hagar’s tent. It isn’t usually wickedness. It is Sarah with a calendar, right about the arithmetic and wrong about God. Name your Hagar’s tent, and give the matter back to God today.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by the free woman Sarah was Isaac, born by promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reads the story figuratively: the two women represent two covenants. Hagar stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem — law-keeping as the way to God — which bears children into slavery. A system of earning acceptance can only produce slaves, however holy its origin.

Allegory? This worries careful readers, rightly. In Paul’s day Alexandrian interpreters like Philo read the Old Testament allegorically in a way that dissolved its history: Abraham became the soul, Sarah virtue, and whether it happened ceased to matter. If Paul did that, anyone could make any text mean anything. But he doesn’t. He has just insisted “it is written that Abraham had two sons” — the history is his premise. He names the mothers, their status and each birth as facts. He isn’t saying the story stands for something instead of happening; he is saying it happened and that God so arranged it that it carries a meaning Christ has now made visible.

Typology. That is typology, not Philo’s allegory — what the risen Christ did on the Emmaus road: “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). If God governs history and knows the end from the beginning, the pattern in a true story is not imposed by the reader but put there by the Author.

Why is Hagar Mount Sinai? Hagar’s descendants, through Ishmael, settled in the desert lands of Arabia (Gen 25:12–18), and Sinai lies there.
